front.title: The Proto eXpressive Format (PXF) and the protowire Encoding Family

abstract.t: This document specifies the Proto eXpressive Format (PXF), a UTF-8 text serialization for messages defined by Protocol Buffers schemas, together with three companion encodings: PB (the existing Protocol Buffers binary wire format, with PXF-specific annotations that constrain how it is produced and consumed), SBE (a fixed-layout binary encoding derived from FIX Simple Binary Encoding), and a response envelope. Collectively these are referred to as the protowire family. This document defines the wire surface sufficient for independent interoperable implementations. It does not define library APIs.

This revision (-01) introduces a set of strictly-additive schema language extensions — type, function, and annotation declarations, a unified annotation use-site syntax, and a structured validation error model — that promote message validation to a first-class schema concern. It also introduces keyed repeated fields: a schema annotation and a strictly-additive PXF surface form for ordered collections of named elements. The additions do not change the PB, SBE, or envelope wire formats.

note.title: Editorial Note
note.t: This revision of draft-trendvidia-protowire updates the document to include the v1.2 Protowire Schema Extensions: three new top-level declarations (type, function, annotation), a unified annotation use-site syntax, and a structured validation error model. The additions are strictly additive; every schema valid under -00 (corresponding to protowire v1.0-v1.1) remains valid under -01. The substantive content of this revision is concentrated in the new Schema Language Extensions section and additions to the Annotation Extensions section and the ABNF appendix; other sections are materially unchanged from -00 and are reproduced verbatim. The corresponding design-rationale document, RFC-001, was ratified on 2026-07-16 and is published in the protowire source repository.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Protocol Buffers is widely deployed for binary serialization of structured data, but its standard text format ("text format", or "prototext") is targeted at debugging and does not address the requirements of human-edited configuration, API integration, or fixed-layout binary streaming. The protowire family covers those requirements while reusing Protocol Buffers schemas as the single source of truth for field identity, types, and numbering.
The family comprises four encodings:

dd.t: A UTF-8 text format with a small, regular grammar; intended for human authoring and machine consumption alike.

The existing Protocol Buffers binary wire format . This document does not redefine PB; it specifies the constraints that a protowire implementation applies on top of PB and the annotation extensions it uses.
A fixed-layout binary encoding derived from FIX Simple Binary Encoding , driven from Protocol Buffers schemas annotated with SBE template metadata.
A versioned response wrapper carrying transport status, application errors, field-level errors, and an opaque payload.

section.t: All four are driven from a single set of .proto schemas. PXF and SBE add field-level and message-level annotations expressed as Protocol Buffers extension options, defined in .

Status of the underlying Protocol Buffers specification. Protocol Buffers does not currently have a finalized IETF standard. The canonical specification is published by Google at https://protobuf.dev/ and, in practice, the protoc reference compiler acts as the de facto specification for behavior the published documentation does not pin down. An IETF effort is in progress to register Protocol Buffers media types ; that draft registers both "application/protobuf" and "application/x-protobuf" (the latter reflecting historical deployment under the experimental "x-" prefix that predates RFC 6648), but does not redefine the wire format. of this document registers a separate "application/protowire-pb" type that signals the additional conformance and annotation requirements specified here.

Relationship to ProtoJSON. Protocol Buffers also defines a JSON mapping commonly called "ProtoJSON" , which serializes messages as JSON objects, represents google.protobuf.Timestamp as an RFC 3339 string, and represents google.protobuf.Duration as a decimal-seconds string with an "s" suffix. PXF () is intentionally distinct from ProtoJSON: PXF targets human authoring and review, supports comments, multi-line strings, and bare-identifier enum values, and uses an entry-list document shape rather than JSON's object-and-comma shape. Where the two formats overlap on semantics — most visibly the use of RFC 3339 for timestamps — PXF intentionally adopts the ProtoJSON convention to reduce the number of disjoint time formats a tooling chain has to support. Implementations are not required to provide ProtoJSON; this document does not specify it.

This document treats both (the language and feature spec) and (the binary wire format) as normative references in their protobuf.dev form, and inherits whatever stability properties those documents and the protoc implementation provide. A future revision of this document SHOULD migrate to an IETF Protocol Buffers reference if and when one is published as an RFC.

section.name: Scope
section.t: This document defines:

list.t: the lexical and syntactic structure of PXF text ();
the constraints that protowire applies to PB binary encoding ();
the SBE wire framing used by protowire ();
the schema-level annotation extensions ();
the schema language extensions for validation, refinement aliases, and metadata annotations (); (new in -01)
the response envelope ();
the conformance requirements that any decoder operating on untrusted input MUST satisfy ().

section.t: This document does not define library APIs, programming-language bindings, code generation strategies, or performance characteristics.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
The following terms are used throughout this document:

dd.t: A Protocol Buffers FileDescriptorSet , together with any annotation extensions defined in .
An independent implementation of the protowire encodings, typically targeting a single programming language.
A complete PXF input: a sequence of bytes that satisfies the production "document" in .
A PXF construct that denotes a single scalar, list, or nested block; see .
A key together with an assignment, map, or block tail; see .
One of the Protocol Buffers types listed in Section 6 of (Timestamp, Duration, the *Value wrappers, etc.) plus the protowire-defined arbitrary-precision numeric types ().
Bytes whose origin is the calling application; not under attacker control.
Bytes whose origin is, or may be, under the control of a party with a goal adverse to the host of the decoding process.

section.t: The following additional terms are introduced in -01:

dd.t: A named refinement of a primitive, enum, wrapper, or message type, declared with the type keyword. See .
A signature for a named validation predicate, declared with the function keyword. Bodies are implemented per-runtime by the consuming validator. See .
A named metadata attachment declared with the annotation keyword, usable at use sites via the @name(args) syntax. See .
A structured value emitted by a function declaration when validation fails, carrying a code, structured parameters, and a fallback message. See .

A runtime component that executes the expressions and function calls appearing in a schema's validation annotations. The engine is selected per project; this document specifies the contract between the schema and the engine, not the engine's internals. See .

section.name: The protowire Family
section.t: A protowire implementation accepts and emits four wire forms for any message defined in a schema: PXF text, PB binary, SBE binary (when the message carries SBE annotations), and Envelope binary (which is itself a PB message).

section.name: Common Schema Layer
section.t: For any schema S, the four encodings represent the same logical value space. Implementations MUST produce wire output that round-trips through every encoding for which the schema is well defined; concretely, for a value v of type T defined in S:

list.t: decode_PB(encode_PB(v)) == v
decode_PXF(encode_PXF(v)) == v
decode_SBE(encode_SBE(v)) == v if T carries SBE annotations
encode_PB(decode_PXF(t)) == encode_PB(v) if t = encode_PXF(v)

section.t: Equality is defined per Section "Message equality" (field-by-field, with proto3 default semantics applied).
A decode that applies pxf.default () has two exceptions to decode_PXF(encode_PXF(v)) == v. Both come from what an absent or null field means, and no text avoids them:

list.t: An unset scalar field with explicit presence and pxf.default (a proto3 "optional" scalar, or a scalar member of a oneof with no member set) reads back holding its default. An absent field with a default means the default, and an encoder leaves such a field out. "null" would keep the field unset (), but writing it is not required.
In a message that declares a "_null" field mask, an unset field with pxf.default reads back either holding its default, if it is left out, or listed in the mask, if it is written "null".

section.t: A decode that applies no annotations has neither exception.

section.name: Wire Equivalence
section.t: Two ports are wire-equivalent for schema S if, for every value v of every message type in S, both ports produce byte-identical PB and Envelope output and parse each other's PXF and SBE output to equal values. Wire equivalence is the contract this document specifies; it is not an API-stability or performance contract.

section.name: PXF Text Format
section.t: PXF is a UTF-8 text format. A PXF document is a sequence of entries denoting a single message value, optionally preceded by a type directive that identifies the schema type the document represents.

section.name: Character Set
section.t: A PXF document is a sequence of bytes that, when interpreted as UTF-8 , yields a sequence of Unicode scalar values.

list.t: A document MUST be valid UTF-8.
Decoders MUST reject documents containing invalid UTF-8 byte sequences with an error.

Decoders MUST reject documents containing Unicode surrogate code points (U+D800 through U+DFFF) or code points above U+10FFFF, regardless of how the surrogate or out-of-range value is expressed (raw bytes that round-trip as such are already excluded by valid-UTF-8 conformance; \uHHHH and \UHHHHHHHH escapes producing those code points are excluded by ).

A leading UTF-8 byte order mark (U+FEFF, encoded as %xEF.BB.BF) MAY be present and MUST be ignored. Subsequent occurrences of U+FEFF are interpreted as ordinary characters and have no special meaning.

section.name: Whitespace and Comments
section.t: The following Unicode scalar values are whitespace: U+0009 (HT), U+000A (LF), U+000D (CR), and U+0020 (SPACE). Whitespace separates tokens but is otherwise insignificant.
PXF supports two comment forms:

list.t: Line comments begin with "#" or "//" and extend to (but do not include) the next U+000A.
Block comments begin with "/*" and end at the next occurrence of "*/". Block comments do not nest.

section.t: Comments MAY appear anywhere whitespace MAY appear. A comment is treated as a single whitespace character for the purposes of tokenization.

section.name: ABNF Grammar
section.t: The PXF surface grammar is given in ABNF . The grammar describes a token stream; whitespace and comments per MAY appear between any two adjacent tokens and are not shown.

figure.sourcecode:
document = *directive *field-entry
directive = type-directive / dataset-directive / proto-directive / named-directive type-directive = %s"@type" 1*WSP identifier named-directive = "@" directive-name *( 1*WSP identifier ) [ block-tail ] directive-name = identifier ; excluding the spec-reserved names ; "type", "dataset", "proto", ; "entry", "table", "datasource", ; "view", "procedure", "function", ; "permissions", and the value ; keywords "null", "true", "false" ; ({{reserved-directive-names}}).
dataset-directive = %s"@dataset" [ 1*WSP identifier ] 1*WSP "(" column-list ")" *( 1*WSP row ) column-list = identifier *( "," identifier ) ; a field name, or a dotted path to a ; field in a sub-message ; ({{the-dataset-directive}}) row = "(" row-cell *( "," row-cell ) ")" row-cell = [ value ] ; a cell means "column = value" ; ({{the-dataset-directive}})
proto-directive = %s"@proto" proto-body proto-body = proto-anon-body / proto-named-body / proto-source-body / proto-descr-body proto-anon-body = 1*WSP "{" proto-message-body "}" proto-named-body = 1*WSP identifier 1*WSP "{" proto-message-body "}" proto-source-body = 1*WSP triple-string proto-descr-body = 1*WSP bytes proto-message-body = <protobuf message-body production from the Protocol Buffers language> ; ({{the-proto-directive}})
entry = field-entry / map-entry field-entry = ( identifier / string ) ( assignment-tail / block-tail ) ; string form: quoted entry name, valid only ; inside keyed repeated fields ; ({{keyed-repeated-fields}}) map-entry = map-key map-tail
assignment-tail = "=" value map-tail = ":" value block-tail = "{" [ any-type-entry ] *entry "}"
map-key = identifier / string / integer / bool
value = string / number / bool / null / bytes / timestamp / duration / identifier / list / block-value
list = "[" [ value *( [","] value ) ] "]" block-value = "{" [ any-type-entry ] *entry "}" any-type-entry = %s"@type" "=" string ; only in a block bound to google.protobuf.Any ; ({{any-blocks}})
number = ( float / integer ) [ precision ] precision = %s"p" 1*DIGIT ; only on a literal bound to pxf.BigFloat ; ({{pxf-annotations}}) integer = [ "-" ] 1*DIGIT float = [ "-" ] 1*DIGIT ( "." *DIGIT [ exponent ] / exponent ) exponent = ( "e" / "E" ) [ "+" / "-" ] 1*DIGIT
bool = %s"true" / %s"false" null = %s"null"
identifier = ident-start *ident-part ident-start = ALPHA / "_" ident-part = ALPHA / DIGIT / "_" / "."
string = triple-string / simple-string
simple-string = DQUOTE *( string-char / escape-seq ) DQUOTE string-char = %x20-21 / %x23-5B / %x5D-7F / utf8-non-ascii ; LF, ", \ excluded
triple-string = 3DQUOTE triple-content 3DQUOTE triple-content = *( %x00-21 / %x23-7F / utf8-non-ascii ) ; any UTF-8 sequence not containing 3DQUOTE
escape-seq = "\" ( simple-escape / hex-escape / octal-escape / unicode-4-escape / unicode-8-escape )
simple-escape = DQUOTE / "\" / "'" / "?" / %x61 / %x62 / %x66 / %x6E / %x72 / %x74 / %x76 ; a b f n r t v hex-escape = "x" 2HEXDIG octal-escape = oct-lead 2OCT-DIGIT ; value <= 0xFF unicode-4-escape = "u" 4HEXDIG unicode-8-escape = "U" 8HEXDIG
bytes = %x62 DQUOTE *base64-char DQUOTE ; 'b' "..." base64-char = ALPHA / DIGIT / "+" / "/" / "=" timestamp = date-time ; per RFC 3339, Section 5.6
duration = ["-"] 1*duration-segment duration-segment = 1*DIGIT [ "." 1*DIGIT ] time-unit time-unit = "ns" / "us" / micro-us / "ms" / "s" / "m" / "h" micro-us = %xC2.B5 %x73 ; UTF-8 of "µs"
OCT-DIGIT = %x30-37 oct-lead = %x30-33 ; ensures \NNN <= 0xFF 3DQUOTE = DQUOTE DQUOTE DQUOTE utf8-non-ascii = <any UTF-8-encoded Unicode scalar value in U+0080..U+10FFFF, excluding surrogates>

section.t: ABNF core productions ALPHA, DIGIT, HEXDIG, DQUOTE, and WSP are imported from Appendix B.1. The case-sensitive string-prefix notation %s is from ; PXF identifiers, keywords ("true", "false", "null"), and the "@type" directive are case-sensitive.
The grammar is LL(1) modulo the lexical disambiguation rules in and :

list.t: An input that begins with four DIGIT followed by "-" is tokenized as a timestamp, not as a negative integer or a bare identifier-prefix.

An input matching ["-"] 1*DIGIT [ "." 1*DIGIT ] time-unit, where the time-unit is one of the literal strings in the grammar above, is tokenized as a duration; the optional leading "-" appears once, before the first segment, never per segment ("-1h30m" is a duration, "1h-30m" is not). A DIGIT-led token that continues past a time-unit into further ALPHA (for example "5seconds", "5sx", "1.5min") is an invalid duration and MUST be rejected as such; it is never an identifier, because identifier productions cannot begin with a DIGIT.

Numeric literals take precedence over identifiers: a leading DIGIT or "-" forces the numeric branch, within which a token that ends in a time-unit is a duration and one that does not is an integer or float, optionally followed by a precision suffix ("p" and 1*DIGIT, as in "1.5p53", "5p64" or "1e5p64"; ). No time-unit begins with "p", so the suffix never makes a token a duration. "+" is not a numeric-branch prefix: the only token it may begin is the identifier "+inf" (), so "+30s" is not a duration.

section.name: Documents and Directives
section.t: A PXF document represents a single message value. Before the body, the document MAY carry zero or more directives. A directive begins with "@" followed by a name. Four directive shapes are given semantics by this document: "@type" names the body's schema-typed message (); "@dataset" carries row-oriented bulk data (); "@proto" carries an embedded protobuf schema (); and "@entry" bundles heterogeneous typed sub-messages () via the named-directive shape (). Directive names beyond the reserved set () are application-extensible.

section.name: The "@type" Directive
section.t: The "@type" directive, of the form

figure.artwork: @type identifier

section.t: names the fully-qualified message type. Decoders MAY require the type directive when the calling application has not pre-bound a target type; decoders MUST ignore the directive when a target type has been pre-bound and the directive matches it, and MUST reject when it does not match.
At most one "@type" directive MAY appear in a document.

section.name: Named Directives
section.t: A named directive has the form

figure.artwork: @<name> *( <prefix-id> ) [ "{" inner "}" ]

section.t: where <name> is an identifier other than the spec-reserved names listed in ; each <prefix-id> is an identifier (possibly dotted); and inner is a sequence of entries syntactically identical to the body of a message block.

The prefix-identifier list is positional; the count and meaning of the identifiers are per-directive-registration. The conventional shape used in the wild is a single prefix identifier naming the inner block's message type (e.g. chameleon's @header chameleon.v1.LayerHeader { ... } preamble, which carries per-file sanity-check fields the resolver enforces against its chain spec). defines a second shape ("@entry") that uses two prefix identifiers.

Named directives carry side-channel metadata that the consumer's runtime interprets — never the body's schema layer. This document defines no <name> beyond those registered in subsections of ; specific names are reserved by other specifications or by applications.
Conformance:

list.t: A decoder that does not recognize a directive name MAY skip the directive after parsing its prefix identifiers and block (if present) for syntactic well-formedness, or MAY reject the document. Implementations SHOULD document which policy they apply.
A decoder MUST NOT attempt to interpret the inner block against the body's schema; the inner block is a self-contained sub-document and is decoded against its own type (if any) by the consumer.
The inner block is parsed by the same entry grammar as a message body (): the same brace-matching, string, and comment rules apply. Braces inside string literals or comments do not close the block.

The number and interpretation of prefix identifiers are specified by each directive's registration. A decoder that recognizes the directive name MUST enforce the registered cardinality. A decoder that does not recognize the name MAY accept any cardinality (the grammar imposes no upper bound).
Multiple named directives MAY appear; their relative order is preserved by decoders that expose a directive list to callers.

A formatter, which rewrites a document's text without changing what it denotes, MUST keep every directive, in document order: "@dataset" with each of its rows, "@proto", "@entry", and every named directive. It writes a named directive's block and a "@proto" body as they were written. It MAY write "@type" first, since "@type" binds no anonymous "@proto" (issue #558).

section.t: A document with no entries denotes the message-typed default value (all fields unset).

section.name: The "@entry" Directive
section.t: The "@entry" directive is the canonical PXF shape for bundling heterogeneous, typed sub-messages alongside (or in place of) a document body. Its form is

figure.artwork: @entry [ <name> ] [ <type> ] [ "{" inner "}" ]

section.t: where <name> is a caller-provided label identifier, <type> is a dotted identifier naming the inner block's message type, and inner is a sequence of entries decoded against <type>. Each prefix identifier is optional; permitted shapes are:

The fourth shape is disambiguated from the second by the presence of a "." in the single prefix identifier: a dotted identifier is interpreted as a type; an undotted identifier is interpreted as a label. Applications that need an undotted type identifier MUST use the third shape with an empty-string label or supply the label explicitly.

"@entry" is consumer-interpreted; this document defines no meaning for the label beyond its preservation in directive order. Typical uses include manifest documents, mixed-type exports, and any case where a document needs to carry several typed values that are not naturally a single repeated field.
Conformance:

list.t: A decoder that recognizes "@entry" MUST accept zero, one, or two prefix identifiers and MUST reject three or more.
A decoder MUST preserve "@entry" occurrences in document order when exposing them to callers. Duplicate labels MAY appear; this document does not impose a uniqueness rule.
An "@entry" with no body block ("{}") denotes the default value of its declared <type>, or an empty anonymous sub-document if <type> is absent.
"@entry" inherits the schema constraint of : <name> MUST NOT be case-sensitively equal to "null", "true", or "false"; <type> MUST refer to a non-conformant-name-free message type.

section.name: The "@dataset" Directive
section.t: The "@dataset" directive is the canonical PXF shape for representing many instances of a single message type in a single document — the protowire-native replacement for CSV. Its form is

where <type> is a dotted identifier naming the row message type; <col1>, <col2>, ... is the column list (at least one column); and each subsequent parenthesized tuple is a row whose values bind positionally to the columns.

Anonymous binding. <type> MAY be omitted when an anonymous "@proto" directive () precedes the "@dataset" in document order. The anonymous schema is consumed as the row message type and the header carries only the column list:
The anonymous "@proto" binding is one-shot per : a second untyped "@dataset" in the same document requires a second preceding anonymous "@proto".

Cell values. A cell holds any value of the value production of , lists ("[ ... ]") and block values ("{ ... }") included. A non-empty cell in column <c> means exactly what the entry "<c> = <value>" means in a message body of <type> (): the same field binding, the same type checks, and the same nullability rules. When <c> is a column path, the entry is written inside the blocks its path names (see Column paths). So a row can carry a sub-message, a repeated field or a map:
A "{}" cell is a present sub-message with every field unset, which an empty cell is not. Before v1.13, cells were limited to scalar values, and list and block cells were rejected.

Cells stay easy to frame. No value contains "(" or ")" outside a string or a comment, so the end of a row is the ")" that matches its "(" with strings and comments skipped, whatever the cells hold. A streaming reader finds row boundaries that way, never by splitting on commas.
Three-state cells. Each row cell denotes one of three states, carried into the bound message via the same semantics as the PXF annotations of :

list.t: An empty cell (no value between two commas, or leading / trailing inside a row, e.g. "(1, , 3)") denotes an absent field. When the bound field carries (pxf.default), the default literal is applied; when it carries (pxf.required), the document MUST be rejected. For a field inside a sub-message, named by a column path, both hold only when the row makes that sub-message present (see Column paths).

A bare "null" literal denotes a present-but-null field. This suppresses (pxf.default). In a column whose field carries (pxf.required) the document MUST be rejected, as for an empty cell: a required field holds a value. The singular-field nullability rules of applied against the field the column names: a field declared on <type>, or for a column path the field its last segment names.
Any other value literal denotes a present field with that value.

section.t: Row arity. Each row MUST have the same number of cells as the header column list. Decoders MUST reject a row whose arity differs from the column count. Trailing-empty shorthand (a row with fewer cells implying absent tail columns) is not permitted in v1.

Column paths. A column entry is a field name declared on <type>, or a dotted path to a field inside a sub-message of <type>: "desc.energy" names the field "energy" of the message-typed field "desc". A row binds as the message body built by grouping its non-empty cells by path prefix. A non-empty cell in column "a.b.c" contributes the entry "c = <value>" inside the block "a { b { ... } }", and every cell of the same row whose column starts with "a." contributes to that same one "a" block. One block per prefix is required, not a style: two blocks for one sub-message bind that field twice, which a body may not do (), so cells written as separate blocks would fail whenever two columns share a prefix.
The first row is the body 'id = "e1" desc { energy = 0.5 tempo { min_bpm = 60 } tags = [ TAG_WARM ] }'. The rules that follow from the grouping:

list.t: A block none of whose cells is non-empty is not written, so its sub-message is absent, as an empty cell in a column naming it would be. In the second row above, "desc" is absent. A sub-message that is present with every field unset is written as a "{}" value cell in a column naming the sub-message, which cannot sit beside columns into it (see below).
"null" in a dotted cell is the entry "c = null" inside the block. The leaf's nullability rules apply, and the enclosing blocks are written, so the sub-messages on the path are present.
Columns may reach different members of one oneof, and several columns may fill the same member. A row that fills two members is rejected, as the body would be.
(pxf.required) and (pxf.default) on a field inside a sub-message apply when the sub-message is present, as in a body, and not when it is absent.

section.t: A header MUST be rejected when:

list.t: the same column appears twice, or one column is a field and another a path inside it ("a" beside "a.b"), since a row could then set one sub-message twice. Sibling paths ("a.b" beside "a.c") are fine. A column path with an empty segment ("a..b", "a.") is rejected as well;
a segment names no field of the message it is resolved against;
a segment other than the last names a field that is not a singular message field: a repeated or map field (a path has no index or key; a value cell on that field is the way to write it), or a scalar;

a segment other than the last names a field whose message type is written as a literal of its own: google.protobuf.Timestamp, google.protobuf.Duration, the google.protobuf wrapper types, pxf.BigInt, pxf.Decimal or pxf.BigFloat. A path into one would expose the type's encoding rather than its literal. The list is closed. pxf.Secret () is not on it: it has a string literal, but its block form is one documents are written in, so a path may go into it, and "pw.hint" names the field the block 'pw { hint = ... }' would. A path may also go into a google.protobuf.Any. It then names the Any's own fields, type_url and value, as a block with no type entry does (), and it cannot reach the fields of the message the Any holds.

section.t: The first rule needs no schema, so a parser that does not bind rows applies it too. The others need <type>, and a decoder applies them when it binds a row. It applies them to every row it binds, whatever the row's cells hold, so a row of empty cells is rejected as well. A table with no rows binds no row, so these rules are not checked against it: a decoder MUST NOT reject a table with no rows for breaking one. A tool such as a linter MAY still report it. A plain column that names no field of <type> is treated the same way. The rules are checked per row because a streaming reader may learn <type> only when its caller binds the first row. Before v1.13, a column entry containing a "." was rejected.

Standalone. A document containing a "@dataset" directive MUST NOT also contain a "@type" directive and MUST NOT contain top-level field entries (). The "@dataset" header is itself the document's type declaration; the rows are the document's payload. A document MAY contain multiple "@dataset" directives (whether of the same or different row types); their relative order MUST be preserved by decoders that expose a dataset list to callers.

Consumer contract. "@dataset" is consumer-interpreted in the same side-channel manner as named directives (): the rows are exposed to callers through a parser API distinct from the body's schema layer. This document does not mandate a single canonical "decode-as-repeated-<type>" semantics; an application that wants that one-liner constructs it on top of the rows API. The schema layer of <type> MUST NOT receive the rows as message body entries.

Streaming consumption. Because "@dataset" is the canonical PXF replacement for CSV, implementations are expected to handle datasets whose row sequence does not fit in memory. Tools MAY expose a streaming row-iteration API alongside (or in place of) the materializing one. A streaming API MUST yield rows in source order, MUST enforce the per-row arity rule and the cell grammar on each row as it is consumed (not deferred to end-of-input), and SHOULD bound its working-set memory by the size of the largest single row plus a small bookkeeping overhead — not by the size of the row sequence. Streaming and materializing APIs that coexist in the same implementation MUST produce byte-identical row sequences for the same input.

Appending. A "@dataset" can be appended to, and that is a supported use: a writer adds a record by writing one complete row after the last, and there is no closing token to rewrite. The row sequence ends only at end of input or at the next directive. Anything else where a row could begin is a decode error, never an end of the sequence. That includes a row whose closing ")" never arrives, which is what an interrupted append leaves behind. This holds for the streaming API as much as the materializing one, so a row cut short by a failed write is reported and does not silently hide the rows appended after it.
Conformance:

list.t: A decoder MUST reject a document where a "@dataset" directive coexists with a "@type" directive or with any top-level field-entry.
A decoder MUST reject a row whose arity differs from the column count.

A decoder MUST reject a row that is not closed before end of input, and MUST reject any token other than "(" or "@" where a row could begin. A streaming API MUST report either as an error at that row, not as the end of the row sequence.
A decoder MUST reject a header that names a column twice, names a field beside a path inside it, or has a column path with an empty segment.

A decoder that binds rows MUST reject a column path that does not resolve against <type>, that goes through a repeated, map or scalar field, or that goes into a type written as a literal, as described under Column paths. It applies these rules when it binds a row, and MUST NOT reject a table with no rows for breaking one.

A decoder MUST bind a row whose header has column paths as the body that groups the row's non-empty cells by path prefix into one block per prefix, and MUST NOT write a block none of whose cells is non-empty.

A decoder MUST bind a non-empty cell as the entry "<c> = <value>" would bind in a body of <type>, and MUST reject a cell that entry would reject (for example, a block in a scalar column). For a column path, the entry is the one the grouping writes inside the path's blocks.

A decoder MUST resolve identifier-shaped cell values against the field the column names (for a column path, the field its last segment names): an enum-typed column accepts an enum value name (); a string-typed column accepts only quoted strings, not bare identifiers.

"@dataset" inherits the schema constraint of : <type> MUST refer to a non-conformant-name-free message type, and each field a column entry names, every segment of a column path included, MUST have a name that is itself non-conformant-name-free.

section.name: The "@proto" Directive
section.t: The "@proto" directive carries an embedded protobuf schema, making the PXF document self-describing. Its form is

figure.artwork: @proto <body>

section.t: where <body> is one of four shapes distinguished lexically:

Anonymous form. The body is a Protocol Buffers message-body production (a sequence of field declarations and nested types) with no surrounding message Name { ... } wrapper and no "package" statement. The anonymous message is consumed as the typed binding of the next directive in document order that requires one and does not carry an explicit type name (e.g. "@dataset" per ). The binding is one-shot.

Named form. The dotted identifier names the message type: the dotted prefix is the package and the final component is the message name. The body is a Protocol Buffers message-body production, identical to the anonymous form. A document with multiple named "@proto" directives binds them into a single document-scoped schema; conflicting type definitions (two "@proto" directives sharing a fully-qualified name with diverging bodies) MUST be rejected.
Source form. The triple-quoted-string body is a complete Protocol Buffers source file with optional "syntax", "package", "import", and one or more "message" / "enum" declarations.
Descriptor form. The bytes-literal body is a base64-encoded google.protobuf.FileDescriptorSet (the pre-compiled form).
Imports. Source-form "@proto" directives that contain "import" statements MUST resolve those imports from one of:

list.t: the Protocol Buffers well-known types under "google/protobuf/": "any.proto", "api.proto", "descriptor.proto", "duration.proto", "empty.proto", "field_mask.proto", "source_context.proto", "struct.proto", "timestamp.proto", "type.proto" and "wrappers.proto", and no other file protoc bundles there (issue #388);
the canonical PXF and SBE schemas ("pxf/annotations.proto", "pxf/bignum.proto", "pxf/secret.proto", "sbe/annotations.proto");
the canonical envelope ("envelope/v1/envelope.proto");
another "@proto" directive in the same document.

section.t: Imports from the filesystem, a remote schema registry, or an external schema supplied to the decoder (such as a tool's -p flag) are NOT permitted from inside a source-form "@proto" body, and neither is any other schema the canonical repository distributes. The list above is exhaustive. An import that does not resolve to one of the four sources above MUST be rejected. The fixtures under testdata/proto-imports/ pin both verdicts (issue #369).

Precedence with external schemas. When a decoder is supplied with an external schema (via a tool's -p flag or a pre-bound descriptor) and the document also carries an "@proto" directive, the embedded schema is authoritative. Decoders MAY verify that the external schema agrees with the embedded one, by comparing the definitions of the message types both of them define. The file each definition lives in is not part of the comparison, since an embedded schema is not a file a decoder was given. A decoder that finds a disagreement MUST either reject the document or report the disagreement to its caller (a warning suffices); either way, a document it decodes is decoded against the embedded schema (issue #371). An external type that the embedded schema does not define can refer to one that it does, as a field's type. When the two definitions of the referred type disagree, decoding through that field against the embedded definition is not possible without rebuilding the external schema, so a decoder that does not rebuild it MUST reject a document whose type reaches such a field (issue #387). Identical definitions raise nothing.
Conformance:

list.t: A decoder MUST support the descriptor form. Decoders MAY support the source, named, and anonymous forms. A decoder that does not support a body shape encountered in a document MUST report an error indicating which shape was rejected; pre-compilation by a separate tool (e.g. protowire compile) is the recommended fallback.
A decoder MUST reject an anonymous "@proto" directive that is not consumed by a subsequent typed directive in the same document.
A decoder MUST reject duplicate fully-qualified type definitions across multiple "@proto" directives in the same document when the definitions diverge.
A decoder MUST reject an "import" inside a source-form "@proto" body that does not resolve to one of the four permitted sources listed above.
"@proto" inherits the schema constraint of : the embedded schema MUST NOT declare a message field, oneof, or enum value whose name case-sensitively equals "null", "true", or "false".

section.name: Reserved Directive Names
section.t: The directive-name production () excludes a set of identifiers reserved by this document. Applications MUST NOT use any of these names for their own named directives (). The reserved set is:

list.t: "type" — names the body's message type ().
"dataset" — row-oriented bulk data ().
"proto" — embedded protobuf schema ().
"entry" — bundle/manifest sub-messages ().

"table" — reserved for a future revision describing the storage shape of tabular data (column types, primary keys, indexes, partitioning, constraints). v1 decoders MUST reject "@table" as an unknown reserved directive.

"datasource", "view", "procedure", "function", "permissions" — reserved for a future revision describing database export/import metadata (data origin, view definitions, stored procedures and functions, access control). v1 decoders MUST reject these as unknown reserved directives.
"null", "true", "false" — value keywords (); excluded to keep the directive-name lexer unambiguous.

section.t: The check is case-sensitive: directive names such as "@TABLE", "@Proto", "@DATASOURCE" lex as ordinary application directives () and are accepted, subject to any application's own naming rules.

Future revisions of this document MAY allocate semantics to the future-reserved names ("table", "datasource", "view", "procedure", "function", "permissions") and MAY add new names to the reserved set. Allocating semantics to a name that was already reserved is not a breaking change because the name was already rejected by v1 decoders; adding a new reservation IS a breaking change and requires a major-version bump.

section.name: Entries and Keys
section.t: An entry binds a key to a value. The key is a field name within the surrounding message type, with the following rules:

list.t: An identifier key matches a field by its proto field name (the lowerCamelCase or snake_case name in the schema, as written; both forms are accepted, and emitters SHOULD use whichever the schema declares).

A string key is permitted in two positions: inside a map<K,V> literal (the map-entry production of ), and as the quoted entry name of a field-entry — the latter is meaningful only inside a keyed repeated field's block (), where it supplies the element's key-field value rather than naming a field. A string key MUST be a UTF-8 string; for map<K,V> fields with non-string K, the string is parsed as a literal of K's type. For a bool K that literal is exactly "true" or "false" (): "1" and "0" are integer literals, and a string key carrying one does not match a bool K.

An integer key is permitted only inside a map<K,V> literal, and matches a map<K,V> field whose K is one of the protobuf scalar integer types (int32, int64, sint32, sint64, uint32, uint64, fixed32, fixed64, sfixed32, sfixed64, bool encoded as 0/1).

A bool key — the keyword true or false, bare — is permitted only inside a map<K,V> literal, and matches a map<bool,V> field. It is the spelling an author naturally writes; the integer spelling above remains valid for the same field. An identifier key inside a map<K,V> literal whose K is bool matches nothing: an identifier names a field, and a map has none, so "t", "TRUE" and "yes" are errors rather than values.

section.t: Canonical spelling of map keys. Because the bare spellings true, false and 123 are a bool key, a bool key and an integer key rather than the strings they resemble, the quotes on a key are meaningful, and a formatter MUST NOT add or drop them where doing so would change what the key denotes. A formatter writes a key bare when the document wrote it bare. A quoted key is written bare when it is identifier-safe — it matches the identifier production of and is not one of the value keywords "null", "true", "false" — and quoted otherwise; in particular a quoted "true", "false" or "null", and a quoted key matching the integer production, stay quoted. Formatters therefore retain whether a map key was written quoted, as already requires of keyed entry names. A marshaller, which has no document spelling to preserve, writes a string key bare under the same identifier-safe test and quoted otherwise, and writes bool and integer keys bare; a formatter and a marshaller thus agree on every key that both can produce (issue #306). The fixture pairs "fmt-keyword-keys" and "fmt-bare-keys" under testdata/map-keys/ pin both directions.
The three entry tails are NOT interchangeable; the grammar in splits them across two productions:

list.t: An assignment-tail "=" binds a scalar, list, or block to a field of an enclosing message type. It is the right-hand side of field-entry and takes an identifier key (= proto field name) or a string key (a quoted entry name, valid only in keyed repeated fields per ; the schema layer rejects it everywhere else). Parsers MUST reject "=" with an integer key at parse time.

A map-tail ":" binds a value to a key of an enclosing map type. It is the right-hand side of map-entry. map-entry MUST NOT appear at document top level (the document represents a proto message, never a map<K,V>); parsers MUST reject ":" at the top level with an error indicating that field assignments use "=".

A block-tail "{ ... }" with no preceding "=" or ":" is permitted only in message context, where the bound field is message-typed; it is equivalent to "= { ... }". Like assignment-tail, it takes an identifier key or a string key (quoted entry name, keyed repeated fields only), and parsers MUST reject a block-tail with an integer key at parse time. Map values that are themselves messages MUST use the explicit form "key: { ... }"; the bare-block form is not accepted in map context.

section.t: Inside a "{ ... }" block the parser cannot statically tell whether the surrounding field is message-typed or map-typed; both field-entry and map-entry are accepted in that position and the message-vs-map disambiguation is performed by the schema-resolution step that runs after parsing.

A repeated field is written with a list value ("tags = [A, B]"). A repeated field MAY be bound more than once. Its value is then the elements of every binding, concatenated in document order, so "tags = [A]" followed by "tags = [B]" denotes the same value as "tags = [A, B]". A decoder MUST reject a repeated field bound to a scalar ("tags = A") or to a block ("items { ... }" or "items = { ... }"). The one exception is the keyed surface form of a keyed repeated field (): its block holds named elements, not a single element.

A singular field, meaning any field that is neither repeated nor a map, MUST NOT be bound more than once in one message body, and a decoder MUST reject the second binding (issue #347). That holds whatever the two bindings are: two different values, the same value twice ("s = "a"" twice), "null" and then a value, or two blocks for one message-typed field ("m { a = 1 }" then "m { b = 2 }", or "m = { ... }" then "m { ... }"). Two blocks do not merge. A oneof's members are singular fields, so a member bound twice is rejected by this rule, and binding a second member of the same oneof is rejected as says. Each message body is a scope of its own: a field bound once in each of two sub-messages, or once in each element of a list, is bound once in each. The fixtures under testdata/duplicates/ pin each case.

A map field MAY be bound more than once in one message body. Its entries are then the entries of every binding, as a repeated field's elements are the elements of every binding. A key, however, MUST NOT occur more than once in one message body's bindings of a map field, and a decoder MUST reject the second occurrence (issue #396). That holds inside one map literal ("labels = { a: "1" a: "2" }") and across two bindings ("labels = { a: "1" }" then "labels = { a: "2" }"), whatever the two values are. Keys compare as values of the map's key type, so for an integer-keyed map "1: "x"" and ""1": "y"" name the same key. As for singular fields, each message body is a scope of its own: the same key in the maps of two list elements, or of two sub-messages, occurs once in each.

section.name: String Literals
section.t: PXF supports two string forms. Both denote sequences of Unicode scalar values.
Simple strings use double-quote delimiters and recognize escape sequences:

figure.artwork: "Hello, world\n"

section.t: Within a simple-string, U+000A (LF) MUST NOT appear unescaped: line continuations are not supported. Decoders MUST reject a simple-string containing a literal LF.
The defined simple escapes are:

figure.artwork: \" U+0022 QUOTATION MARK \\ U+005C REVERSE SOLIDUS \' U+0027 APOSTROPHE \? U+003F QUESTION MARK \a U+0007 BELL \b U+0008 BACKSPACE \f U+000C FORM FEED \n U+000A LINE FEED \r U+000D CARRIAGE RETURN \t U+0009 CHARACTER TABULATION \v U+000B LINE TABULATION

section.t: Numeric escapes:

figure.artwork: \xHH two hex digits, denotes the byte 0xHH \NNN three octal digits, value MUST be <= 0xFF; denotes the byte 0xNN \uHHHH four hex digits, denotes Unicode scalar U+HHHH \UHHHHHHHH eight hex digits, denotes Unicode scalar U+HHHHHHHH

section.t: The \uHHHH and \UHHHHHHHH forms MUST denote a Unicode scalar value: the code point MUST be in U+0000..U+10FFFF and MUST NOT be a surrogate (U+D800..U+DFFF). Decoders MUST reject otherwise.
The interpretation of \xHH and octal escapes depends on the target field type:

list.t: When the surrounding string literal is bound to a proto3 string-typed field, the result of escape expansion MUST be valid UTF-8. Decoders MUST reject a string-typed value whose escape-expanded byte sequence is not valid UTF-8 ().
When the surrounding string literal is bound to a proto3 bytes-typed field, no UTF-8 constraint applies.

section.t: Triple-quoted strings ("""...""") begin with three U+0022 characters and end at the next occurrence of three consecutive U+0022 characters. Inside a triple-quoted string:

list.t: Escape sequences are NOT interpreted; backslashes are literal.
If the byte immediately following the opening """ is U+000A, that LF MUST be removed by the decoder.

After leading-LF stripping, if every non-empty line preceding the closing """ shares a common leading-whitespace prefix, that prefix MUST be removed from each such line. The "leading whitespace" is the longest sequence of U+0020 and U+0009 characters at the start of a line; lines that consist exclusively of whitespace do not constrain the prefix.

section.t: The output of triple-quote processing MUST be valid UTF-8 when bound to a string-typed field; the same UTF-8 conformance rule in applies.

section.name: Bytes Literals
section.t: A bytes literal is the lowercase letter "b" immediately followed by a double-quoted body containing only base64 characters :

figure.artwork: b"SGVsbG8sIHdvcmxkIQ=="

section.t: Decoders MUST accept both the standard base64 alphabet and the URL-safe alphabet Section 5; padding ("=") is OPTIONAL and MUST be tolerated whether present or absent. Decoders MUST reject input containing characters outside both alphabets and "=". Whitespace is NOT permitted inside the body.
Backslashes inside b"..." are NOT interpreted as escape introducers.

section.name: Numeric Literals
section.t: Integers are sequences of decimal digits, optionally preceded by "-". Hexadecimal, octal, and binary integer literals are NOT defined in this version.

Floats are decimal-point or exponent forms; see the ABNF in . An integer or float may end in a precision suffix, "p" and a bit count after any exponent; only a pxf.BigFloat field accepts one (). The literal "1." is a valid float (integer part 1, empty fractional part); the literal ".5" is NOT (no integer part). This restriction is intentional: an unprefixed "." is reserved for future qualified-key syntax.
The target field type determines the numeric domain:

list.t: For fixed-width integer fields (int32, int64, uint32, uint64, sint32, sint64, fixed32, fixed64, sfixed32, sfixed64), decoders MUST reject literals whose value falls outside the field's representable range.

For float and double fields, decoders MUST accept literals in the IEEE 754 representable range; values that round to +Inf or -Inf are rejected unless explicitly written as the identifiers "inf", "+inf", "-inf", "nan".

A NaN has many IEEE 754 encodings, so which one is written is fixed here. A decoder reading the identifier "nan" into a float or double field MUST store the canonical quiet NaN: 0x7FF8000000000000 for a double, 0x7FC00000 for a float. A PB or SBE producer that writes from a language value, such as a floating-point type bound to a struct field, MUST write any NaN in that canonical form. A producer that writes a message's fields, such as a generated or dynamic message, MUST write them as they are, so that a NaN read from PB keeps its encoding (issue protowire-java#161).

For fields of the well-known types pxf.BigInt and pxf.Decimal (), decoders MUST preserve the literal's exact value, including, for Decimal, the exact scale: the literal "1.00" decodes to a Decimal with unscaled value 100 and scale 2, distinct from "1.0" or "1". A pxf.BigFloat is binary, and most decimal literals have no exact binary value, so a decoder reads one as the nearest value at the precision its suffix states, or at 256 bits without one ().

section.t: The number of digits in any single numeric literal is bounded; see .

section.name: Booleans, Null, and Identifier Values
section.t: The literals "true" and "false" denote the boolean values; "null" denotes the null value. All three are case-sensitive. A "null" literal:

list.t: When bound to a singular message-typed field, MUST clear the field.

When bound to a singular scalar field with explicit presence, as protobuf defines it (a proto3 "optional" scalar, a scalar member of a oneof, a proto2 "optional" scalar, or in an editions file a scalar whose field_presence feature is EXPLICIT), MUST leave the field unset. The field is present-but-null: pxf.default is not applied to it.

When bound to a singular scalar field without explicit presence (a proto3 scalar declared without "optional", or in an editions file a scalar whose field_presence feature is IMPLICIT), MUST be rejected. Such a field has no unset state, so a null would read back as the field's zero value. A field that must be nullable is declared "optional", or as its wrapper type (e.g. google.protobuf.StringValue).

When bound to a proto2 "required" field, or an editions field whose field_presence feature is LEGACY_REQUIRED, MUST be rejected. The field has explicit presence, but leaving it unset would make the message invalid in protobuf binary, which requires the field to be set.

When bound to a field that carries pxf.required, or the @required annotation, MUST be rejected, whatever the field's type and presence. A required field holds a value: neither absent nor null satisfies it ().

When bound to a list-typed (repeated) field, a map field included, MUST be rejected; so MUST a null list element and a null map value, whatever the map's value type: list elements and map entries are not nullable. In protobuf binary a map entry without a value reads back as the value type's zero value, so the null could not be kept.

When bound to a member of a oneof, message or scalar, makes that member the one the body chose. A body that also writes another member of the same oneof writes two members, and MUST be rejected as any such body is ().

section.t: An identifier appearing as a value denotes an enum value name when the target field is enum-typed. Decoders MUST reject unknown enum names unless the schema declares the field with open enum semantics, in which case the unknown name is preserved in the message's unknown-fields set.
Because "true", "false", and "null" are reserved value keywords, a protobuf schema MUST NOT declare an enum value, message field, or oneof bearing any of those names; see .

section.name: Timestamps and Durations
section.t: A timestamp literal is an RFC 3339 date-time production. The lexer recognizes a timestamp by lookahead: an input matching the regular expression /^[0-9]{4}-/ at a position where a value is expected MUST be tokenized as a timestamp. This rule disambiguates against the identifier and integer productions.

The choice of RFC 3339 aligns with the ProtoJSON serialization of google.protobuf.Timestamp, which uses the same format. A PXF timestamp literal and the ProtoJSON string form of the same Timestamp value are byte-identical except for the surrounding ProtoJSON quote characters. PXF duration literals are NOT byte-compatible with ProtoJSON's Duration form (a decimal-seconds string with an "s" suffix); PXF retains the multi-segment unit form ("1h30m500ms") because it is materially easier to read in human-authored documents.

Decoders MUST accept timestamps with arbitrary fractional-second precision up to nanoseconds. Decoders that target a fixed-precision representation (typically google.protobuf.Timestamp, which has nanosecond resolution) MUST reject literals exceeding that precision rather than silently truncating.
A duration literal is a sequence of one or more segments, each consisting of a numeric magnitude followed by a unit suffix:

figure.artwork: 30s ; 30 seconds 1h30m ; 1 hour 30 minutes 500ms ; 500 milliseconds 1.5h ; 1.5 hours 2µs ; 2 microseconds (alternative form: 2us) -1.5s ; minus 1.5 seconds

section.t: google.protobuf.Duration is signed, and so is the literal: a negative duration is written with a single leading "-" before its first segment, applying to the whole literal ("-1h30m" is minus ninety minutes). Encoders MUST emit a negative Duration in that form and MUST NOT emit a sign per segment or a "+"; a decoder MUST bind "-1h30m" to seconds = -5400 and, when a fractional segment yields nanoseconds, to seconds and nanos of the same sign, as google.protobuf.Duration requires. "-0s" denotes zero. Whether a leading "+" is admitted is not settled by this revision; it is not part of the grammar, no encoder writes it, and decoders that accept it are lenient rather than conformant.

A duration literal holds a signed 64-bit count of nanoseconds, about 292 years, while google.protobuf.Duration reaches about 10,000 years. An encoder MUST write a value that does not fit that count as a block () holding its exact seconds and nanos. It MUST NOT write a longer, wrapped or truncated literal.

The defined units are "ns", "us", "µs", "ms", "s", "m", and "h", denoting nanoseconds, microseconds (twice; "us" and "µs" are semantic equivalents), milliseconds, seconds, minutes, and hours respectively. Day, week, month, and year units are NOT defined and MUST NOT be inferred.

section.name: Lists
section.t: A list value is a sequence of values delimited by "[" and "]". Elements MAY be separated by "," or by intervening whitespace alone (including newlines), or by both:
A trailing comma is permitted.
List values bind only to repeated fields, to fields whose Protocol Buffers type is a list-shaped well-known type, and to list elements within other lists.

section.name: Blocks and Map Tails
section.t: A block value "{ entry-list }" denotes a nested message when the surrounding context is message-typed, and a map literal when the surrounding context is map-typed. Within the block, keys are interpreted against the nested message's or map's schema. Blocks nest to arbitrary depth subject to the limit in .
A nested message field is bound with "=" (or with the bare-block form, which is its abbreviation):

figure.artwork: address = { city = "Berlin" zip = "10115" } address { city = "Berlin" zip = "10115" } ; same value

section.t: A map field is bound with "=" between the field name and the block, but the entries inside the block use ":" because each entry is a key-of-the-map-to-value pair:
Decoders MUST reject "=" inside a map block and ":" inside a message block ().

Within either kind of block, entries are separated by whitespace, newlines included, and by nothing else: in the ABNF in entries are juxtaposed with no separator token. A "," or ";" between two entries of a block is not whitespace, and a decoder MUST reject it. The comma separates list elements only. The fixtures under testdata/blocks/ pin both rejections (issue #312).

section.name: Keyed Repeated Fields
section.t: A keyed repeated field is a repeated message-typed field for which the schema designates a scalar key field of the element message, via the pxf.key annotation ():
The annotation makes the field's collection-of-named-elements semantics visible to the schema layer: entry order is list order, and each element's identity is the value of its key field.

section.name: Schema Placement
section.t: pxf.key is subject to bind-time checks in the sense of , over the scope of ; tools that bind a descriptor for PXF use MUST reject a schema in which:

list.t: pxf.key is set on a field that is not a repeated field of message type (scalar fields, map fields, and singular message fields do not accept it);
the annotation value does not name a field of the element message; or
the named key field is not a singular field of type string.

section.t: This revision restricts the key field to type string. A future revision may extend the key-field type set (for example to the integer map-key types); such an extension would be additive.

section.name: Keyed Surface Form
section.t: A keyed repeated field MAY be written as a block whose entries are named blocks — one field-entry per element, in list order:

Each entry's name supplies the element's key-field value; the entry's block is the element message body. An entry name MAY be a string literal (the string alternative of field-entry in ), which keeps keys that are not identifier-shaped expressible:

Because a block-tail is an abbreviation of "= { ... }" (), an entry MAY equivalently be written "name = { ... }"; any non-block value on a named entry is an error, since the element type is a message.
The existing anonymous list form remains valid for the same field, with the key field written explicitly:

figure.artwork: children = [ { id = "greeting" type = "Label" } ]

section.t: The general repeated-field concatenation rule () applies unchanged: a document may bind the same keyed field more than once (in either form), and elements concatenate in document order.

Entry names are atoms. The ident-part production permits ".", so "user.name { }" is a legal unquoted entry name; tools that build symbol paths from entry names MUST treat each name as one opaque key, never as path segments.

section.name: Decoding
section.t: When decoding a keyed block:

list.t: The entry name (unquoted value, for string-literal names) populates the element's key field.

Two entries in the same block whose names are equal after unquoting are duplicate keys, and decoders MUST reject the block. The comparison is on the denoted string value: "foo" quoted and foo bare are the same key.

The empty string is not a valid key value. A quoted entry name "" is a decode error, and so is an explicit empty-string assignment to the key field of any element of a keyed repeated field, in either surface form.
An explicit assignment to the key field inside a named entry's block that disagrees with the entry name is a decode error. An assignment that agrees is redundant but legal.

The entry name is a binding of the key field, so a named entry's block cannot undo it. An agreeing assignment is the one exception to the rule of that a singular field is bound once. Binding the key field to "null" disagrees with the entry name and is a decode error. When the key field is a member of a oneof, binding any other member of that oneof in the block, to a value or to "null", writes two members and is a decode error (). The anonymous list form has no entry name, so neither case arises there, and an element whose key is absent stays legal.

section.t: A quoted entry name anywhere other than inside a keyed repeated field's block is grammatically well-formed but MUST be rejected by the schema layer: a string entry name never names a field, so it is only meaningful as a key.

Schema-tolerant parsers (parsers that operate without a bound schema) carry entry names through unchanged, along with whether the name was quoted, so that formatting round-trips; the checks above that require schema knowledge are then diagnostics of whatever later stage binds the schema. In tolerant decode modes, the duplicate-key, empty-key, and key-conflict errors above SHOULD be surfaced as diagnostics rather than hard failures.

section.name: Encoding and Canonical Form
section.t: Emitters MUST use the keyed block form for a keyed repeated field whenever every element's key field is present, non-empty, and distinct within the emitted collection, and MUST use the anonymous list form otherwise (elements with absent keys, or duplicate keys where the schema layer tolerates them, can only be represented anonymously).
In keyed form:

list.t: An entry name is emitted unquoted whenever the key is identifier-safe — it matches the identifier production of and is not one of the value keywords "null", "true", "false" — and quoted otherwise. Formatters MUST canonicalize a quoted identifier-safe name to its unquoted spelling.
The key field is not additionally emitted inside the entry's block; formatters MUST drop a redundant (agreeing) explicit key-field assignment when canonicalizing.

section.t: Formatters with schema access MUST canonicalize an eligible anonymous-form binding to the keyed form under the same rules.
The pb and SBE binary encodings (, ) are unaffected: a keyed repeated field is a plain repeated field on the wire, and the key travels as an ordinary field of the element message.

section.name: Schema Constraints
section.t: The PXF lexer reserves "true", "false", and "null" as value keywords (), and "type" as the type-directive name (). A protobuf schema whose declared names collide with any of these keywords produces fields, oneofs, enum values, or named-directive registrations that are unreachable from PXF surface syntax: the keyword wins in the tokenizer, so an assignment such as "field = null" always resolves to the null-literal branch, and an enum value literally named "null" can never be selected by name. PXF therefore constrains schemas as follows.
A protobuf schema bound for PXF use MUST NOT declare any of the following with a name case-sensitively equal to "null", "true", or "false":

list.t: a message field (any field of any message);
a oneof (the oneof identifier itself, not its member fields, which are governed by the message-field rule above);
an enum value.

section.t: In addition, a named-directive registration () MUST NOT use a name listed in the reserved-directive-name set of . This is already enforced by the directive-name production of .

The check is case-sensitive. Names such as "NULL", "True", or "FALSE" lex as ordinary identifiers and are unaffected. Names that begin with a digit (e.g. "1null") are already forbidden by the protobuf identifier rule and need no PXF-specific restriction.
Conformance:

list.t: Tools that bind a protobuf descriptor for PXF use (encoders, decoders, codegen plugins, schema linters, schema registries) MUST reject a non-conforming schema at bind time. A conforming decoder MUST NOT silently produce bindings in which a declared enum value, field, or oneof is unreachable from PXF surface syntax.
Implementations SHOULD report the offending element by its fully-qualified protobuf name (e.g. "trades.v1.Side.null") and SHOULD point at this section.

Schemas that violate this constraint were never round-trippable through PXF. Rejecting them on upgrade surfaces a pre-existing latent bug rather than introducing one; this document therefore defines no migration accommodation.

section.name: Well-Known Type Shapes
section.t: A PXF codec recognizes the well-known types below by their fully-qualified names, and reads and writes their fields directly to give them their literal forms and other special handling. A schema may declare a message with one of these names itself: the canonical schemas are copied into many repositories. Such a declaration has to have the shape the codec relies on.

A protobuf schema bound for PXF use MUST NOT declare a message with one of these names unless it declares each listed field with that name and type, singular unless the table says repeated. Protocol Buffers presence ("optional") does not change a field's shape.

texttable.title: Well-Known Type Shapes
texttable.c: bytes unscaled, int32 scale, bool negative
bytes mantissa, int32 exponent, uint32 prec, bool negative

section.t: A value of google.protobuf.Timestamp, google.protobuf.Duration, a google.protobuf wrapper type, pxf.BigInt, pxf.Decimal, or pxf.BigFloat is written either as its literal or as a block naming its fields. A singular field, each element of a list, and each value of a map may take either form, and the two forms denote the same value.

A pxf.Secret MAY omit hint and fingerprint, and each that it declares MUST be a singular string. A message MAY declare further fields, and this section places no requirement on them. Field numbers are not part of the shape, since PXF binds fields by name.
Conformance:

list.t: A tool that binds a protobuf descriptor for PXF use MUST reject a schema that violates this constraint at bind time, as for , and SHOULD report the message by its fully-qualified name.

An implementation MAY offer a way to bind without these checks, and an encoder need not run them. A message with one of these names that does not have the shape is then an ordinary message: the implementation MUST NOT give it a literal form or other well-known-type handling, and MUST report any failure as an ordinary decode or encode error.

A schema that violates this constraint could not be used reliably before this rule, because a codec would fail on the first value of that type. Rejecting it surfaces a pre-existing latent bug; this document therefore defines no migration accommodation.

section.name: Scope of Bind-Time Checks
section.t: The constraints above, and every other check this document requires at bind time — the pxf.key placement rules of , the pxf.default placement rules of , and the oneof rules of — are stated against "a schema". A protobuf descriptor spans more than one file, so this section fixes what that means.

The schema a bind-time check covers is the .proto file declaring the bound descriptor together with its transitive imports. A tool binding a descriptor MUST apply every bind-time check of this document to each file in that closure, and MUST report a violation found in any of them.
A file reached more than once through the import graph is checked once. A violation is attributed to the file that declares the offending element, not to the file that was bound.

The narrower reading — that a check covers only the file declaring the bound descriptor — does not satisfy the conformance requirements those checks state. A decoder recurses into message-typed fields whose types are declared in imported files, and a misplaced annotation on such a type is as unhonorable there as it is in the bound file, but no document need ever make the diagnostic appear: the annotated field is only consulted when its containing message is present. The result is precisely the outcome forbids in its first conformance bullet, reached by a different route.

A third reading was considered and rejected: covering only the message types a decoder can reach from the bound descriptor by following message-typed fields. It cannot be evaluated at bind time. A field of type google.protobuf.Any names its payload type in the document, and the binding tool resolves it through a type resolver at decode time, so the reachable set is not a function of the descriptor. The import closure is a property of the descriptor alone, and is therefore the only scope a bind-time check can be stated against.
Conformance:

list.t: A tool that binds a descriptor MUST NOT report a schema conformant on the basis of having checked only the declaring file.
The closure is the import closure, not the set of files a document happens to exercise. A file in the closure is checked whether or not any field of the bound message refers to a type it declares.

This scope makes one non-conforming file poison every file that transitively imports it. That is intended: an annotation no implementation can honor is worth surfacing wherever it is reachable, and a widely-imported file is where a dead annotation does the most damage.

section.t: Non-normative: the closure of any file that uses these annotations includes pxf/annotations.proto and, through it, google/protobuf/descriptor.proto, which no PXF document can reference. Implementations that re-check on every decode rather than once per bound descriptor will pay for that traversal repeatedly; memoizing the result per file descriptor is the expected implementation and costs less than the single-file traversal it replaces.

section.name: Any Blocks
section.t: A block bound to google.protobuf.Any MAY begin with a type entry: "@type", "=", and a string, the type URL. The block may be the value of a singular Any field, an element of a repeated Any field, or a value of a map whose values are Any. The string is the Any's type_url, stored verbatim. The decoder resolves it to a message type through a type resolver supplied out of band. The rest of the block is a body of that type, and the Any's value field holds the body's Protocol Buffers binary encoding.
A block bound to google.protobuf.Any without a type entry is a body of google.protobuf.Any itself, whose entries are type_url and value:

figure.artwork: payload = { type_url = "type.googleapis.com/acme.v1.ErrorDetail" value = b"CCo=" }

section.t: Conformance:

list.t: A decoder MUST reject a type entry that is not the first entry of its block, a second type entry in one block, and a type entry in a block not bound to google.protobuf.Any (a nested message, a map block, or the document body).

A decoder MUST reject a block whose type URL it cannot resolve to a message type, including when it has no type resolver. It MUST NOT read the remaining entries as fields of google.protobuf.Any instead.
The body after the type entry is decoded as any body of its type is: the limits of apply to it, and so do the annotation rules of .

A parser that does not bind a schema cannot tell which blocks are bound to Any. It accepts a type entry as the first entry of any block, and the rules above apply when the document is bound. It MUST reject a type entry anywhere else in a block.

An encoder MAY write an Any in either form, and writes the type URL verbatim. It MUST write the type entry and body only when its resolver maps the stored type URL to a message type and decoding the body it writes gives exactly the stored value bytes. Otherwise it MUST write type_url and value. A reader compares an Any by its bytes, so a body that decodes to other bytes changes the message with no error. Unknown fields, field and map order, explicitly written zeros, and values the PXF form does not spell are where the two differ (issue #501). How an encoder makes the comparison is its own choice, and one that writes every Any as type_url and value conforms.

section.name: PB Binary Encoding
section.t: The protowire PB encoding is the Protocol Buffers binary wire format with no protowire-specific changes to the wire grammar. This document does not redefine PB.
Constraints applied by protowire:

list.t: Annotation extensions defined in are encoded as Protocol Buffers field options on the relevant FieldOptions, MessageOptions, and FileOptions messages. Their field numbers are reserved ().

Decoders MUST enforce the limits in on PB inputs. In particular, the depth limit applies to nested submessages, groups, and map entries, except a big-number message a decoder binds to a native number (); the length-prefix limit MUST be enforced before allocation.
A protowire emitter SHOULD produce fields in field-number order; decoders MUST accept any field order, per the existing PB rules.

An emitter MAY write the entries of a map field in any order, and decoders MUST accept any order. Where PB bytes from two implementations are compared, as the conformance suite does, map entries are compared in key order: false before true, integer keys by value, and string keys by their UTF-8 bytes. A deterministic emitter that writes entries in that order produces bytes that compare equal with no reordering.

Where PB bytes are compared, fields are compared in field-number order too, at every level of nesting. The records of one field keep their relative order, so a repeated field's elements do not move, and nothing else is normalized. An emitter that writes some fields out of field-number order, as one that writes a oneof after the other fields does, still compares equal to one that follows the SHOULD above.

section.name: SBE Binary Encoding
section.t: The protowire SBE encoding is a subset of FIX Simple Binary Encoding . An SBE message is generated for any Protocol Buffers message annotated with sbe.template_id; the schema-level identifiers come from sbe.schema_id and sbe.version on the file ().
Field-level annotations sbe.length and sbe.encoding control fixed-byte-length string and bytes fields and primitive-type narrowing respectively ().

section.name: Character Encoding
section.t: An SBE string field holds UTF-8 text, and decoders reject one that is not valid UTF-8, as for every other string field. FIX SBE makes US-ASCII the default encoding of a char array, and US-ASCII text is valid UTF-8. A FIX SBE schema can declare another encoding with the characterEncoding attribute; this document defines no annotation that carries one. A tool that imports a FIX SBE schema MUST therefore map a char type to a string field only when its characterEncoding is absent or names US-ASCII or UTF-8, and MUST map any other char type to a bytes field of the same length. Mapping it to a string would make every value with a byte outside UTF-8 fail to decode.

section.name: Fixed-Length Arrays
section.t: A FIX SBE type whose length attribute is greater than 1 is a fixed-length array of its primitive type; a length of 1, or none, is a single value. A tool that imports a FIX SBE schema MUST map a uint8 or int8 array of length N to a bytes field with sbe.length N, which occupies the same N bytes of the block, and MUST map a char array as described in the previous section. It MUST reject an array of any other primitive type, since no field this document defines holds one; importing it as a single value would misplace every later field in the block. A tool that exports a FIX SBE schema MUST write a bytes field with sbe.length N as a uint8 array of length N, and a string field with sbe.length N as a char array of length N. A bytes field written as a char array would be imported again as a string field. A bytes field with sbe.length 1 is exported as a single uint8 and imported again as a narrowed integer field: its byte in the block is unchanged, and its field type is not.

section.name: Header and Block Length
section.t: Every SBE message on the wire is preceded by an 8-byte message-header carrying the schema's blockLength, templateId, schemaId, and version, in little-endian byte order. Decoders MUST validate, before reading any field of the body:

list.t: data.length >= HEADER_SIZE + wire_block_length

wire_block_length >= template_block_length, where template_block_length is the value the decoder's compiled schema specifies for this template. A wire block strictly smaller than the template block length MUST be rejected. A wire block strictly larger MUST be accepted (forward compatibility for additive schema evolution).

the header's templateId and schemaId name the message being decoded. sbe.template_id is unique only within a schema, so the templateId alone does not identify a message. A decoder given the message to decode MUST reject a header whose templateId differs from that message's sbe.template_id, or whose schemaId differs from the sbe.schema_id of the message's file. A decoder that finds the message from the header MUST look it up by schemaId and templateId together, and MUST reject a pair its compiled schemas do not hold. Without this check, bytes written for one schema's message decode as another schema's message with the same templateId, and when that message's block is no longer, its fields are misread without error.

section.name: Repeating Groups
section.t: Each repeating group is preceded by a group-header carrying blockLength and numInGroup. Before iterating any group, decoders MUST validate:

list.t: pos + GROUP_HEADER_SIZE <= data.length
count multiplied by wire_block_length does not overflow 64-bit unsigned arithmetic
pos + GROUP_HEADER_SIZE + count * wire_block_length <= data.length
If count > 0, then wire_block_length > 0. A wire_block_length of 0 with a non-zero count MUST be rejected before any per-element allocation.

section.name: Variable-Length Data
section.t: Variable-length data ("varData") fields follow the fixed block, each preceded by a length prefix per the schema's varDataEncoding. Decoders MUST validate that pos + LENGTH_PREFIX_SIZE + length <= data.length before reading the data.

section.name: Annotation Extensions
section.t: protowire defines extensions on Protocol Buffers FileOptions, MessageOptions, and FieldOptions. Field numbers are allocated from the reserved range described in .

section.name: PXF Annotations
section.t: The PXF annotations apply to FieldOptions:

pxf.required: when true, decoders MUST reject a PXF document in which the annotated field is absent, and one in which it is bound to "null". A required field holds a value; a field that may be left without one is not required (). The annotation is not valid on a member of a oneof; see .
