pxf.default: when set, the value is a PXF literal (parsed by the same rules as a value in any entry). Decoders MUST treat an absent annotated field as if the document had supplied the default literal. The default applies only to absent fields, not to fields explicitly set to "null" or to the proto3 zero value. The annotation carries exactly one literal, so it is valid only on fields a single literal can denote; placement constraints are specified in .

Both rules apply in every message body a document writes, not only at the top level: the body of a singular message field, each element of a list of messages, each value of a map whose values are messages, and the body of a google.protobuf.Any written with "@type". A body is checked against its own message type, and a field bound to "null" has no body to check.

Both rules depend on knowing which fields a document wrote, so they bind a decoder's presence-tracking decode, the entry point that reports field presence to its caller. An implementation MAY also offer a decode that tracks no presence, and that decode does not apply these rules: it accepts a document with an absent pxf.required field and leaves an absent pxf.default field unset. An implementation MAY let a caller turn the rules off on a presence-tracking decode, so that the caller can apply them itself, for example to the result of merging several documents. Documentation of any entry point that does not apply these rules MUST say so.

pxf.key: names the key field of a keyed repeated field. The value is the proto field name of a singular string-typed field of the element message. The annotation is valid only on repeated message-typed fields; placement constraints and the decode, encode, and canonicalization semantics it enables are specified in . The annotation affects only the PXF text surface — pb and SBE wire outputs are unchanged.

The schema-level constraints of apply independently of these annotations: a field, oneof, or enum value whose name collides with a reserved PXF keyword is non-conforming regardless of whether pxf.required or pxf.default is set.

The well-known types pxf.BigInt, pxf.Decimal, and pxf.BigFloat are defined in (this is the proto/pxf/bignum.proto file in the canonical repository). They provide arbitrary-precision signed integer, exact decimal, and binary floating-point representations respectively, encoded over PB as length-delimited unsigned big-endian magnitudes plus sign and scale fields.

A pxf.Decimal's value is (-1)^negative × unscaled × 10^(-scale). The scale is part of a PXF literal but not of the value, so what a PB producer writes depends on what it holds. A producer that writes a message's fields, such as a generated or dynamic message, MUST write them as they are: "1.00" read from text and written by such a producer has unscaled 100 and scale 2. A producer that writes from a language value, such as an arbitrary-precision type bound to a struct field, MUST write the value in reduced form, whether or not that type holds a scale: the smallest scale that is not negative and represents the value exactly, with no leading zero bytes in unscaled. 1.00 is written as unscaled 1 and no scale, 5 × 10^2 as unscaled 500 and no scale, and a zero with no fields set. A reader MUST accept every form and MUST NOT treat a reduced Decimal as a different number (issue protowire-cpp#97). A producer of the reduced form whose scale would exceed MaxNumericLiteralDigits MUST fail with an error.

A pxf.BigFloat's value is (-1)^negative × mantissa × 2^exponent, mantissa an unsigned big-endian integer, rounded to prec bits of precision with ties to even: a mantissa wider than prec bits denotes that rounded value (issue #410). prec 0 or a zero mantissa (empty, or only zero bytes) is zero. A producer MUST encode a zero, at any prec, with an empty mantissa and exponent 0, keeping its prec and negative, so that a zero has one PB encoding: the one a decoder stores when it reads a zero literal. A decoder still reads any zero mantissa as zero, whatever the exponent (protowire-go#196). In PXF text a BigFloat is a numeric literal that carries its precision, as a "p" and a bit count after the number ("0.10000000000000001p53"; the precision production of ), so that both its value and its precision survive the text (issue #406):

list.t: Writing. A producer of PXF text writes N significant decimal digits, where N is the number of decimal digits of 2^prec plus one, rounded to nearest with ties to even, followed by "p" and prec. It writes the digits as C's "%g" conversion does with precision N: trailing zeros removed, in exponent form ("1.79769313486231590773e+308p64", at least two exponent digits) when the decimal exponent is below -4 or at least N, and positionally otherwise. A zero is written "0p" and prec, or "-0p" and prec when negative is set, so that its precision and sign survive; only a zero whose prec is 0 is written without a suffix, "0" or "-0" (issue #410). N is the smallest digit count for which every prec-bit value is recovered by reading its literal back at prec bits (measured on issue #406: one digit fewer lost 9,157 of 20,000 random 53-bit values; with N, value and precision were unchanged after three round trips for every one of 35,600 random values from 24 to 13,000 bits).

Reading. A decoder reads a literal with a precision suffix at exactly that many bits, rounding to nearest with ties to even, and one without a suffix, which a person may write, at 256 bits. It stores mantissa as the value's significand as a prec-bit integer (its top bit set), exponent as the value's binary exponent minus prec, and prec as the precision read at. A zero literal stores an empty mantissa and exponent 0, prec as the precision its suffix states (0 without one), and negative for a leading "-". A decoder MUST reject a suffix whose precision is zero, or whose N exceeds MaxNumericLiteralDigits (), before allocating anything for it. N exceeds a limit L exactly when prec exceeds floor((L - 1) / log10(2)), 13603 at the default, so a decoder compares the suffix with that bound, rejecting one of more digits than the bound has without converting it, and never computes 2^prec.
A precision suffix on a literal bound to any field that is not a pxf.BigFloat is grammatically well-formed but MUST be rejected by the schema layer, naming the field.

section.t: PB to PXF to PB therefore preserves every BigFloat's value, its sign, and its prec, zeros included (issue #410). It does not preserve a mantissa's bytes as written: the reading rule stores the significand as a prec-bit integer, so a mantissa that was not normalized, or was wider than prec bits, comes back normalized to the same value. A value at MaxBigFloatExponent may print as a literal whose exact value lies just past the bound; the bound applies to the value after rounding to the read precision (), so that literal reads back. Reading a literal at any precision other than the one it was written at instead rounds twice: the two such read rules measured on issue #406 lost 0.3% to 0.5%, and 5% to 8%, of values above 256 bits. The fixtures under testdata/bigfloat/, generated with exact rational arithmetic, pin both directions (issue #393).

The well-known type pxf.Secret is defined in the proto/pxf/secret.proto file in the canonical repository. It holds a sensitive string, value, and two optional strings that describe the secret without revealing it: hint, what the secret is, and fingerprint, a non-reversible identifier of it. A pxf.Secret is written in either of two forms. A string literal sets value alone: 'pw = "x"'. A block names the fields: 'pw { value = "x" hint = "database password" }'. Each element of a list, and each value of a map, may take either form. Protecting the value in memory is left to the consumer, not the codec.

section.name: Default Placement
section.t: pxf.default carries exactly one PXF literal, so the fields it can populate are the fields a single literal can denote. Like pxf.key (), it is subject to bind-time checks in the sense of , over the scope of ; tools that bind a descriptor for PXF use MUST reject a schema in which pxf.default is set on:

list.t: a repeated field. One literal cannot denote a list, and the annotation has no grammar for element separation or for the empty list;
a map field. One literal cannot denote a map, and the annotation has no grammar for keys;
a group field; or

a message-typed field whose type is not one of google.protobuf.Timestamp, google.protobuf.Duration, the nine google.protobuf wrapper types (BoolValue, BytesValue, DoubleValue, FloatValue, Int32Value, Int64Value, StringValue, UInt32Value, UInt64Value), pxf.BigInt, pxf.Decimal, or pxf.BigFloat. These are the message types a PXF literal can denote (; the wrapper types take the literal of the type they wrap, and the arbitrary-precision types take a numeric literal). For any other message type there is no literal for the annotation to carry.

section.t: pxf.default is valid on every singular scalar field, on every enum field, and on the message types enumerated above. On an enum field the literal is either a value name or the decimal value number.

The constraint is on placement, not on the literal. A literal that does not parse as the annotated field's type — "abc" on an int32 field — is a decode-time error raised where the default is applied, not a bind-time rejection. Placement is determinable from the descriptor alone, whereas rejecting the literal at bind time would oblige every binding tool to implement the value parser.
Conformance:

list.t: Tools that bind a protobuf descriptor for PXF use MUST reject a non-conforming placement at bind time, independently of what any document contains, and over the whole scope of . A decoder MUST NOT defer the diagnostic to the first document that leaves the annotated field absent: a schema whose annotated field happens to be present in every document it decodes would then carry a meaningless annotation indefinitely without one. Restricting the check to the file that declares the bound message reaches that same outcome for an annotated field of an imported type, and is equally non-conforming.
Implementations SHOULD report the offending field by its fully-qualified protobuf name (e.g. "trades.v1.Order.tags") and SHOULD point at this section.

Implementations MUST NOT invent a semantics for a rejected placement. In particular, a single literal on a repeated field MUST NOT be applied as a one-element list: the resulting PB output would differ from that of an implementation that rejects the schema, for the same schema and the same document.

A pxf.default in one of these placements never had honorable semantics — there was no literal the decoder could have applied. Rejecting it on upgrade surfaces a pre-existing latent bug rather than introducing one; as with , this document defines no migration accommodation.

section.t: A field that satisfies the above but is a member of a oneof carries the additional constraints of .

section.name: Required and Default
section.t: pxf.required and pxf.default MUST NOT both be set on one field. pxf.default says an absent field takes a value, and pxf.required says an absent field is an error, so a document omitting the field has no single meaning: the result would depend on which check an implementation ran first. Tools that bind a descriptor for PXF use MUST reject such a schema, over the scope of . "pxf.required = false" requires nothing and does not conflict with pxf.default.
As with , rejecting such a schema on upgrade surfaces a pre-existing latent bug rather than introducing one.

section.name: Oneof Members
section.t: Setting any member of a oneof clears the others, so the per-field reading of "absent" that pxf.required and pxf.default are otherwise defined against does not hold inside a oneof: a member is absent whenever a sibling was chosen. Both annotations therefore take additional constraints there.
pxf.default MAY be set on a member of a oneof, subject to:

list.t: the default applies only when NO member of the oneof is present in the document. When any member is present the default MUST NOT be applied — applying it would clear the member the document supplied, destroying input;
a member bound to "null" counts as present for this test, consistent with the rule above that "null" suppresses a default; and
at most one member of any one oneof may carry pxf.default. Tools that bind a descriptor for PXF use MUST reject a schema in which two or more members of the same oneof carry it, over the scope of .

section.t: The last constraint exists because the alternative is an ordering rule. With two annotated members and an empty document, some member's default must win; deciding by declaration order would make reordering two field declarations silently change what a document decodes to, and deciding by field number would do the same on renumbering. Rejecting the schema is the only outcome that does not attach meaning to a detail authors are free to change.

pxf.required MUST NOT be set on a member of a oneof; tools that bind a descriptor for PXF use MUST reject such a schema. Read per-field, it requires that one specific arm always be chosen, which makes every other arm of the oneof undecodable. Its only coherent reading — that the oneof must be set to something — is a property of the oneof rather than of any member, and this revision defines no annotation at that scope. A future revision MAY add one; forbidding the member placement now keeps that addition additive rather than a reinterpretation of an existing annotation.
Conformance:

list.t: A decoder MUST NOT apply a oneof member's pxf.default over a present sibling. An implementation that tests presence per field without regard to oneof membership does exactly that, and is non-conforming.

These placements bound cleanly before this revision and decoded destructively: a document choosing one arm decoded as though it had chosen another, and a document choosing a valid arm was rejected for the absence of a different one. As with , rejecting such a schema on upgrade surfaces a pre-existing latent bug rather than introducing one.

section.name: SBE Annotations
section.t: SBE annotations apply at three scopes:
sbe.schema_id and sbe.version identify the schema as a whole. sbe.template_id MUST be unique among messages within a schema.

sbe.length specifies a fixed byte length for string- or bytes-typed fields. Values longer than the limit MUST be truncated by emitters, a bytes field at the limit and a string field at the last character boundary at or before it, so that a truncated string is still valid UTF-8 (). A byte-exact cut can split a multi-byte character, and every strict decoder then rejects the whole message (issue #495). A limit shorter than a string's first character leaves the field empty. Values shorter than the limit, and the bytes a character-boundary cut leaves over, MUST be padded with U+0000 bytes; decoders MUST trim trailing U+0000 bytes when populating string fields and MUST NOT trim them when populating bytes fields.

sbe.encoding narrows a Protocol Buffers numeric type to a smaller SBE primitive. The defined values are: "int8", "int16", "int32", "int64", "uint8", "uint16", "uint32", "uint64", "float", "double". Emitters MUST reject values that fall outside the narrowed type's range; decoders MUST sign-extend or zero-extend per the SBE primitive when populating the wider Protocol Buffers field.

section.name: Schema Extension Annotations
section.t: A new family of annotations is defined in package protowire.schema.v1 to support the schema language extensions specified in . These annotations are declared, not extended onto FieldOptions individually — they participate in the unified annotation framework defined in and , and they lower to the carrier extension described in .
The framework-defined annotations are:

c.spanx: rule: expression, code: string = "", message: string = ""

section.t: The bracket-form annotations (pxf.required) and (pxf.default) defined in -00 retain their semantics unchanged. Their extension field numbers did change: -00 assigned them 50000 and 50001, inside an unregistered range; they are 1314 and 1315 in this revision, within the block registered to protowire (see ). @required and @default defined here are the canonical surface forms going forward; the bracket forms remain valid input that decoders MUST accept indefinitely.

section.name: Schema Language Extensions
section.t: This section is new in -01.

section.name: Overview
section.t: The schema language defined in provides messages, fields, oneofs, enums, services, and methods. This document adds three further top-level declarations to the surface a protowire-conformant schema MAY contain:

dd.t: A named refinement alias bundling a base type with zero or more validation rules. See .
A signature for a named validation predicate whose body is provided by the consuming runtime. See .
A declaration of a metadata attachment usable via the @name(args) use-site syntax. See .

section.t: Each declaration is package-scoped, importable across files, and lowers into the standard FileDescriptorSet representation defined in . The wire format is unaffected: the lowered descriptor uses custom options carried in the protowire-reserved extension number range, transparent to consumers that do not import the carrier schemas.

section.name: Reserved Keywords
section.t: The following identifiers are introduced as contextual keywords by -01:

Each MUST be recognized as a keyword only at the start of a top-level declaration (file scope). In every other position — message names, oneof names, field names, enum-value names, service names, rpc names — the parser MUST accept the same word as an identifier. Implementations SHOULD use the parser's grammar production to distinguish the two contexts; lookahead at the file-scope production is sufficient.

The contextual treatment preserves complete backward compatibility: every schema valid under -00 (protowire v1.0 or v1.1) that uses type, function, or annotation as a message, oneof, field, or enum-value name remains valid under -01 without modification. No source-level incompatibility is introduced.

The character @ (U+0040) is reserved as a sigil introducing an annotation use site. Outside string literals and comments, an occurrence of @ MUST be followed by an identifier and MAY introduce an annotation use site as defined in .
The word expression is a parameter-type designator usable only inside annotation X(arg: expression) declarations (); elsewhere it MUST be treated as a regular identifier.

The word this is bound only inside engine-language bodies of @validate(...) and similar annotations. Protobuf parsers capture those bodies opaquely (per ) and MUST NOT lex this as a keyword in protobuf source.

section.name: Type Declarations
section.t: A type declaration introduces a named refinement of a base type:

figure.artwork: type-decl = "type" ws name ws "=" ws type-ref ws [ annotation-list ] ";" type-ref = qualified-ident qualified-ident = name *( "." name )

section.t: type-ref MUST resolve to one of: a Protocol Buffers primitive type (string, bytes, int32, int64, uint32, uint64, sint32, sint64, fixed32, fixed64, sfixed32, sfixed64, float, double, bool); an enum type; a message type; a well-known wrapper type (google.protobuf.StringValue, google.protobuf.Int32Value, etc.); or another type declaration.
This revision (-01) prohibits repeated and map<K,V> as type-ref. A future revision MAY relax this prohibition.

The optional annotation-list attaches refinement rules and other metadata to the type. By convention, at least one @validate(...) annotation appears, expressing the constraint the type adds beyond its base type's constraints.
Type declarations MUST be uniquely named within their package. Forward references within a file are permitted; cyclic references MUST be rejected by the parser.

section.name: Composition Semantics
section.t: When a type declaration D names another type declaration B as its base, D's constraints AND with B's constraints at every use site. This is the only composition operator; there is no override, intersection, or removal mechanism. Composition is transitive: a chain A → B → C accumulates constraints from A, then B, then C in that order at any field declared as type C.

Composition MUST NOT change the underlying data type. A derived type's base MUST resolve to the same primitive, enum, wrapper, or message kind as its ancestor's; deriving an int32 type from a string-based type declaration is a parse error.

section.name: Use at Field Sites
section.t: A field whose declared type names a type declaration MUST be processed as follows by validators:

list.t: The field's underlying wire type is that of the type declaration's resolved base type, unchanged.
For each composition step in the type's chain, the corresponding refinement rules are appended to the field's validation rule list in base-to-derived order.
Subsequent rules MAY be added at the field site via field-level annotations.

section.t: The complete rule list for a field is evaluated as specified in .

section.name: Function Declarations
section.t: A function declaration specifies the signature of a named validation predicate:

figure.artwork: function-decl = "function" ws name ws "(" [ param-list ] ")" [ ws option-list ] [ ws annotation-list ] ";" param-list = param *( "," ws param ) param = name ws ":" ws type-ref option-list = "[" option *( "," ws option ) "]"

section.t: Function declarations carry no body. The body MUST be provided by the consuming runtime through a registration mechanism specified in . The signature alone is the contract between the schema and the runtime.

section.name: Return Contract
section.t: Every function declared per -01 returns a pair of values: a boolean result and an optional structured violation. The contract is:

list.t: On success, the function returns the equivalent of (true, null).
On failure, the function returns (false, V) where V is a Violation as defined in .

section.t: The specific syntax for expressing this pair in any given runtime language is per-runtime; the contract is what crosses the schema/runtime boundary.

section.name: Parameter Types
section.t: The parameter type-ref MUST resolve to a primitive type, an enum type, a message type, or a type declaration. This revision does not permit repeated, map<K,V>, or expression as parameter types.

section.name: Function References at Validation Sites
section.t: Function calls appear inside expression-typed annotation arguments (see ); this revision defines no other position at which engine expressions occur. The compiler SHALL scan each captured expression body for qualified identifiers and string literals under the Protocol Buffers lexical rules — characters that cannot begin or extend a Protocol Buffers token, such as engine operators, act solely as separators — and treat every maximal occurrence of a qualified identifier immediately followed by ( as a call site, with arity equal to its count of top-level commas plus one (zero for empty parentheses).

A call site whose name resolves to a function declaration in scope (same file or imported) MUST be emitted into the descriptor's Expression.calls field, and its arity MUST match the declaration — a mismatch is a compile-time error attributed to the call's source span. A call site whose name does not resolve MUST be one of the builtins of : it MUST NOT be emitted into Expression.calls, and any other unresolved name is a compile-time error attributed to the callee. Consumers MAY therefore rely on Expression.calls being complete with respect to declared functions and free of builtins.

Every maximal qualified identifier not followed by (, other than this, true, false and in, is an enum value reference. The compiler MUST resolve it from the annotated declaration's scope and emit it into Expression.enum_values once per distinct spelling, with the resolved enum type, value name and number; one that does not resolve to an enum value is a compile-time error attributed to its span. Consumers MUST NOT re-resolve these names.

section.name: Annotation Declarations
section.t: An annotation declaration specifies a named use site for metadata:

figure.artwork: annotation-decl = "annotation" ws name ws "(" [ annot-param-list ] ")" ";" annot-param-list = annot-param *( "," ws annot-param ) annot-param = name ws ":" ws annot-param-type [ ws "=" ws default-value ] annot-param-type = "expression" / "string" / "int32" / "int64" / "float" / "double" / "bool" / "bytes" / "any" / qualified-ident default-value = literal / qualified-ident / expression-body

section.t: A default-value takes the form an argument bound to the parameter would: an expression-body for an expression-typed parameter, and a literal or qualified identifier for every other type. An expression default is captured, checked and lowered exactly as such an argument (), except that its names resolve from the annotation declaration's scope. A check that needs the type this binds to is made at each use site that leaves the parameter to its default.

The annot-param-type value expression indicates that the corresponding argument at use sites is a rule in the expression language of rather than a typed Protocol Buffers literal; the parser captures it as text () and the compiler then parses the capture under that language.

The any parameter type accepts any literal value that the consuming target permits; specific compatibility is enforced at the lowering layer. Message literals bound to any parameters require the explicit type-name form (see ).

Annotation declarations are themselves declared in schema; the framework-defined annotations listed in reflect the canonical set distributed with this specification, but user-declared annotations participate in the same machinery.

section.name: Annotation Use Sites
section.t: A use site is introduced by the @ sigil:

figure.artwork: annotation = "@" qualified-ident [ "(" [ annot-arg-list ] ")" ] annot-arg-list = annot-arg *( "," ws annot-arg ) annot-arg = [ name ws "=" ws ] annot-arg-value annot-arg-value = literal / qualified-ident / expression-body annotation-list = 1*annotation

section.t: Use-site arguments MAY be positional or named. Named arguments MAY follow positional ones; positional MUST NOT follow named.

section.name: Literal Values
section.t: Non-scalar argument values take one of three literal forms (see ): a list literal (["US", "CA", "GB"]), a message literal (myco.commons.Money{currency: "USD", units: 5}), or an enum-value reference (a qualified identifier, resolved at link time).

A message literal's type comes from the annotation parameter's declared type; when the parameter — or, recursively, the message field being initialized — is typed any (or google.protobuf.Any), the explicit leading type name is REQUIRED. When a concrete message type is declared, the type name is OPTIONAL; if present it MUST resolve to exactly the declared type. The type is never inferred from the value's shape.

Field initializers use the field's declared name with a mandatory colon, separated by commas without a trailing comma; each field appears at most once, and an unknown field name is an error. The text-format liberties (colon-less nested blocks, semicolon separators, repeated-field repetition, bracketed type URLs) are not part of this grammar. Repeated fields take list-literal values; map fields are not supported in this revision. Lists are homogeneous, MAY nest, and MAY be empty; expression bodies never appear inside literals.

section.name: Engine Expressions
section.t: An argument bound to an expression-typed parameter is not parsed under the schema grammar of this section; it is captured as text and then parsed under the expression language of . Because an argument's parameter binding is not known until annotation resolution, argument parsing is capture-then-classify:

list.t: The parser captures every annotation argument as raw source text. An argument extends to the first , or ) at zero delimiter depth: (), [], and {} pairs MUST balance, and string literals (Protocol Buffers lexical forms) are opaque to the scan. The scan is character-level, tracking only string-literal boundaries and delimiter depth, so engine operators that are not Protocol Buffers tokens (||, &&, <=, !) pass through unexamined. An unbalanced delimiter or an unterminated string literal MUST be reported as an error attributed to the argument. The capture MUST be non-empty.

An argument that begins with an identifier followed by = — where the token after = is not itself = — is a named argument; the name and = are consumed before capture. Expression fragments beginning with an identifier followed by == are unaffected.

At resolution time, an argument bound to an expression-typed parameter keeps the captured source verbatim, trimmed of leading and trailing whitespace. Quotation marks are NOT stripped: a quoted string bound to an expression parameter is a string-literal expression, which is not a boolean and so is an error (). Every other argument MUST re-parse as a literal or qualified identifier (); any other shape is an error.

section.t: Once bound, the capture is parsed under : the compiler checks the grammar, that every call resolves to a declared function or a builtin, arity (), and that the rule is not visibly something other than a boolean; a capture that fails is a compile-time error attributed to the offending token.

section.name: Expression Language
section.t: The body of every argument bound to an expression-typed parameter — the rule of @validate, and any other expression parameter a schema declares — is written in one fixed language, defined here, the same in every engine and every implementation. (RFC-001 Section 5.4, resolved 2026-09-07; the ratified text left the body to the engine.)

A validation engine evaluates the rule of @validate and no other expression argument. An expression parameter of a user-declared annotation is data for the tool that owns that annotation: a compiler checks it as it checks any rule and lowers it to the annotation carrier, and an engine MUST NOT report a violation from it. A rule meant to be enforced at validation time is written in @validate. (RFC-001 Section 5.4, resolved 2026-10-29.)
Grammar, over the Protocol Buffers lexical forms for identifiers and for integer, float and string literals:

figure.artwork: expr = or or = and *( "||" and ) and = unary *( "&&" unary ) unary = "!" unary / cmp cmp = term [ ( "==" / "!=" / "<=" / ">=" / "<" / ">" ) term ] / term "in" term term = INT / FLOAT / STRING / "true" / "false" / list / "this" *postfix / call / enumref / "(" expr ")" postfix = "." IDENT "(" args ")" ; builtin, method form call = IDENT *( "." IDENT ) "(" args ")" ; declared function, or ; builtin in function form enumref = IDENT *( "." IDENT ) ; enum value; not ; followed by "(" args = [ expr *( "," expr ) ] list = "[" [ term *( "," term ) ] "]"

section.t: this is the only bound identifier. There is no field selection: this.name is not an expression; a rule over a message's fields is a declared function taking the message. A call whose name resolves to a visible function declaration dispatches to the engine's registry (); otherwise the name MUST be one of the builtins below. A builtin's method form this.m(a, ...) is the same call as its function form m(this, a, ...).

An enumref names an enum value: an identifier run not followed by (, other than this, true, false and the operator in. It resolves from the scope of the annotated declaration exactly as an enum-typed annotation argument does: by the value's scoped name (MODE_MATCH, pkg.MODE_MATCH) or in the enum-qualified form (Mode.MODE_MATCH). A reference that resolves to nothing, or to anything but an enum value, is a compile-time error. Its value is the enum value's number. The compiler records each reference resolved in the descriptor's Expression.enum_values; an engine takes the number from that record and MUST NOT resolve a name itself.
Builtins. This is the complete set; an engine MUST NOT accept any other name in an expression argument, and a compiler MUST reject a call to any other name.

texttable.c: int: Unicode code points of a string, bytes of a bytes value, elements of a list or map
bool: whether the pattern matches anywhere in the receiver (unanchored)
the engine-native current instant ( rules 2 and 5)
bool: whether the receiver is a floating-point NaN; false for every integer
bool: whether the number is a declared value of the receiver's enum type
bool: whether no two elements are equal under ==

section.t: Typing and evaluation. The language is dynamically typed: a compiler checks syntax, name resolution, arity, and that a rule is not visibly something other than a boolean; an engine checks operand kinds when it evaluates. && and || short-circuit and require boolean operands; ! requires a boolean operand. == and != compare numbers by value regardless of representation, strings, booleans, and temporal values of the same kind; <, <=, > and >= order numbers, strings (byte-wise), and temporal values of the same kind. A floating-point NaN follows IEEE 754: it equals no number, itself included, so == is false and != is true; it is unordered, so <, <=, > and >= are false whichever side it is on; none of these is an evaluation error. So this >= 0.0 && this <= 1.0 refuses NaN, but !(this < 0.0) and this != 0.0 accept it; a rule that must refuse NaN in every shape says !this.is_nan(). Infinities are ordinary ordered values. in requires a list on its right and tests membership with ==. defined() requires an enum value (this bound from an enum, or an enum value reference); on any other receiver, an integer included, it is an evaluation error. unique() compares every pair of elements with ==; a pair that cannot be compared is an evaluation error, and two NaNs are never duplicates. Any other combination is an evaluation error: the rule fails, and the violation's fallback message carries the engine's error text. The statically visible cases (wrong builtin arity; a builtin in function form with no receiver argument; a visibly non-boolean rule) are compile errors as well.

A rule is a boolean: its result, and each operand of !, && and ||, MUST be one. A compiler MUST reject one of these positions when its term, looking through parentheses, is a string, number or list literal, an enum value reference, size() or now(), or is this alone where this binds to a whole collection (a field-level rule on a repeated or map field), an enum, or a scalar other than bool. Every other term passes, including a declared function (a predicate), this bound to a message (a google.protobuf.BoolValue binds as a bool), and this where the compiler does not know the binding.

The language has no field selection on this, no temporal or duration literals, no arithmetic, no ternary, no comprehensions and no string formatting. Each of those is either a declared function or a future revision of this section; extending the language is a specification change, never an engine extension.

section.name: Placement
section.t: Annotations attach to the immediately-adjacent declaration. Placement is hybrid:

list.t: On block declarations (message, service, rpc, enum, oneof), annotations MUST be leading — appearing on the lines preceding the keyword.

On non-block declarations (type, function, field, enum-value), annotations MUST be trailing — appearing on the same or following lines after the declaration's terminating component, before the terminating semicolon.

section.t: Schemas MAY stack multiple annotations on a single target; they evaluate in source order.

section.name: Coexistence with Bracket Options
section.t: The pre-existing [(qualified-ident) = value] field-option syntax defined in and used by (pxf.required) / (pxf.default) in -00 is preserved unchanged. Annotations and bracket options MAY coexist on the same field, but the two forms lower to disjoint descriptor surfaces: bracket options lower to their declared extend google.protobuf.*Options extensions exactly as written, annotations lower only to the schema-extension carrier, and a compiler MUST NOT synthesize one surface from the other. In particular, @required and @default do NOT emit (pxf.required) / (pxf.default): a consumer reading only the -00 extension numbers observes bracket-written options and nothing else, so deployments MUST upgrade carrier-aware consumers before migrating schemas from brackets to annotations. When both forms of the same semantic appear on one field with conflicting values, a compiler MAY warn; it MUST NOT reconcile them.

section.name: Presence Semantics
section.t: Validation operates over the three-state presence model already specified for PXF in -00 (, "Field presence: set, null, absent"). This subsection restates the model from the validation layer's perspective:

texttable.c: Each rule in the field's rule list is evaluated against the value.
The field's rule list is NOT evaluated. A field with @required is never null: a decoder rejects the null ().
The field's rule list is NOT evaluated.
A Violation with code required is emitted in a layer prior to rule evaluation.
The value v is substituted; rules are evaluated against v.

section.t: For fields inside a oneof group, rules attached to inactive variants MUST NOT be evaluated. Only the active variant's rules apply.

For repeated fields whose element type is a type declaration, the type's rule list is evaluated per element. Field-level rules attached via the field's own annotation-list are evaluated against the collection.
For map<K,V> fields, value rules apply per value; key rules apply per key when the key's declared type is a type declaration.

section.name: Well-Known Type Binding
section.t: Six rules define what the identifier this binds to inside a rule, by the kind of the value's declared type:

list.t: For a well-known wrapper type (google.protobuf.StringValue etc.), this binds to the unwrapped scalar value when the wrapper is set; the rule is NOT evaluated when the wrapper is null.

For google.protobuf.Timestamp and google.protobuf.Duration, this binds to the engine-native temporal value — parallel to wrapper unwrapping, so rules read naturally (this > now()). Engines MUST support the comparison operators <, <=, ==, >=, > between temporal values of the same kind. now() is a builtin of ; the language has no temporal or duration literal, so a rule that needs one declares a function taking the temporal value. As with wrappers, the rule is NOT evaluated when the field is unset.

For google.protobuf.Any, this does not unwrap: it binds to the structured value. The expression language has no field selection, so the canonical type_url refinement is a declared function taking the Any and comparing type_url in its implementation. Engines MUST NOT auto-unpack the payload: unpacking requires resolving the payload type against a descriptor pool at evaluation time, and its result silently changes as pools grow.
For any other message type, this binds to the message instance. A rule over the message's fields is a declared function taking the message; no rule selects a field in the expression itself.
Engine builtins that observe the current time (e.g. now()) MUST be run-stable: every evaluation within the production of one Report observes the same instant.

For an enum type, this binds to the value's number, and a rule compares it with integer literals or enum value references. The number keeps its enum type, which only defined() reads; every operator sees the number alone.

section.t: These rules pin evaluation-time meaning only; they do not change descriptor lowering — a type declaration always records its literal base-type name.

section.name: Evaluation Order and Result Aggregation
section.t: For a given field, rules evaluate in source-list order: base-type refinements first (in the order their declarations appear in the type chain), then field-level annotations.

By default, the validator SHALL evaluate every rule on every relevant field of the message instance and aggregate all resulting violations into a single Report (see ). An engine-level option MAY provide a fail-fast mode that terminates at the first violation; the collect-all mode is the conformance-mandated default.

When rules are evaluated against a @default-substituted value (the absent-with-default row of the presence table above), every resulting Violation MUST carry rule kind DEFAULT, superseding the VALIDATE or TYPE_REFINEMENT kind the same rule would carry for a producer-set value, and actual_value MUST carry the substituted default. Such a Violation reports a schema-authoring error — the declared default fails the field's own rules, so no producer input can trigger it and no producer change can fix it. Tooling MAY reject such defaults at schema-compile time; a schema that passes that check never yields a DEFAULT Violation at runtime.

section.name: Recursion Depth
section.t: Nested-message validation is depth-limited. The root message is at depth 0; each message-typed value entered adds 1. The normative default limit is 64, configurable per project via the max_recursion_depth field of the engine configuration (); a configured value of 0 means the default.

At the limit the engine neither errors nor silently truncates: it emits a fail-closed synthetic Violation with code protowire.depth_exceeded for the subtree it did not enter, sets truncated = true on the Report, and — in collect-all mode — continues with the siblings. The depth definition, the default, and the at-limit behavior are normative; the enforcement mechanism is implementation-defined.
The protowire. violation-code namespace is reserved for specification-defined codes; user schemas and engines MUST NOT mint codes in it.

section.name: Streaming RPC Validation
section.t: Validation over streaming RPCs is per-message: each message is validated independently as it crosses the wire, under the same rules as unary payloads. The receiver MUST validate each message before delivering it to application code; the sender MAY additionally validate before transmission. There is no stream-scoped rule surface in this revision (aggregate invariants across a stream's messages are an open issue; see ).

The first invalid message terminates the stream with an error carrying the Report; there is no lenient mode and no rollback of previously-delivered messages. Status mapping is direction-asymmetric. For gRPC transports, the reference mapping is: a request-direction violation maps to INVALID_ARGUMENT; a server-produced response caught by the sender's pre-send check maps to INTERNAL; a client-side receiver check surfaces as a local error without a wire status. The Report travels in google.rpc.Status.details as a google.protobuf.Any.

section.name: Sensitivity Classification
section.t: The framework annotation sensitive () marks a value as sensitive. It is classification, not protection: wire encoding, storage, programmatic access, and validation semantics are unaffected. How a sensitive value is protected (encryption, key management) is out of scope for the schema layer.

@sensitive attaches to fields, to type declarations (where it macro-expands to every consuming field, like any other type-attached annotation), and to messages (where it applies transitively through message-typed fields).
Consumers MUST observe the following minima:

list.t: Rendering surfaces (editors, log formatters, diagnostic output) MUST redact sensitive values, rendering the placeholder [REDACTED] in place of the value.

Validation engines MUST withhold the offending value from emitted Reports: actual_value is left absent and value_redacted is set (), keeping redaction distinguishable from the three-state absence semantics.
Documentation generators MUST NOT emit values or examples for sensitive declarations; an @example on a sensitive declaration is a compile-time warning.

section.t: @sensitive lowers through the standard annotation carrier (); it has no dedicated descriptor surface.

section.name: Error Model
section.t: A Violation is a structured value with the following abstract shape:

texttable.c: A stable, machine-readable identifier for the failure mode.
Structured parameters relevant to the failure.
A human-readable message used when no locale catalog entry matches code.

section.t: Functions emit Violations on failure. params is populated from exactly two sources: the Violation returned by a declared function (), whose implementation authors its params, and specification-defined synthetic Violations (protowire.depth_exceeded carries limit; see ). For Violations produced by inline expression rules, engines MUST leave params empty: an expression is a rule in the fixed language of , and no mapping from expression shapes to parameter names is defined. A rule that requires structured parameters for catalog interpolation is declared as a function.
The engine MUST further enrich each emitted Violation with at least the following context:

texttable.c: Structured path into the message instance: a segment list carrying field name, field number, and — where applicable — one typed subscript (repeated index, or a map key in its declared key type). The path is never a dotted string.
Type-alias chain from base to derived, when the Violation was produced by a TYPE_REFINEMENT rule.
The value the rule was evaluated against, in a typed representation (see below). Absent when the value is withheld under , in which case value_redacted is set.
The position in the originating .proto source.
One of VALIDATE, REQUIRED, DEFAULT (rule evaluated against a @default-substituted value; see ), TYPE_REFINEMENT.
True when the violated rule applies to the map key itself rather than the value addressed by the final path segment's subscript.

section.t: A subscripted map segment in a field path addresses the entry's value. When a rule is evaluated against the map key itself, the engine MUST set for_key: a key violation and a value violation on the same entry otherwise carry identical paths, and neither the rule kind nor the violation code is required to disambiguate them.

section.name: Report Wire Shape
section.t: The on-wire shape of the aggregate Report is specified normatively by protowire/proto/schema/v1/report.proto in the protowire source repository. It is a runtime artifact — plain proto3 messages carrying no descriptor extension numbers — so all ports emit interchangeable reports across PXF, PB, and the envelope. Summary of the shape:

list.t: Report carries the validated message_type, the list of EnrichedViolations, the execution mode (collect-all or fail-fast), the truncated flag (), engine name/version, and wall-clock evaluation time.

EnrichedViolation carries the causal Violation (code, params, fallback_message) plus the enrichment fields of the table above: the structured FieldPath (typed subscripts), the type_chain, the typed actual_value, the value_redacted flag, the source location, the rule kind, and the for_key flag. Rule-kind enum values are RULE_KIND_-prefixed on the wire.

Values (actual_value and params entries) use a dedicated typed Value oneof — null, string, int64, uint64, double, bool, bytes, enum-value name, packed message, or list — deliberately not google.protobuf.Struct's value type, which folds integers to double, cannot carry bytes, and erases the distinction between null and absent.

section.name: Localization
section.t: When rendering a Violation to a human audience, implementations SHOULD substitute params into a locale-specific template selected by the Violation's code. The catalog of (locale, code, template) tuples is registered with the validator at initialization time. Catalogs are defined in schema using framework-provided annotations whose shape is described in .
On catalog miss, implementations MUST fall back to fallback_message. The fallback is always present and is the engine author's chosen default.

section.name: Lowering to FileDescriptorSet
section.t: Implementations MUST lower the -01 constructs to the standard FileDescriptorSet representation specified in , augmented with custom option extensions carried in protowire-reserved field numbers. The schemas for these extensions are specified in protowire/proto/schema/v1/descriptor.proto and summarized below.

section.name: Extension Number Allocation
section.t: The number range 1327 through 1346 is reserved by -01 for schema-extension carriers. Allocated in this revision:

texttable.c: AnnotationList (named per kind: file_annotations, message_annotations, field_annotations, enum_annotations, enum_value_annotations, service_annotations, method_annotations, oneof_annotations)
FileOptions, MessageOptions, FieldOptions, EnumOptions, EnumValueOptions, ServiceOptions, MethodOptions, OneofOptions

section.t: The annotation carrier shares wire number 1327 across all eight target messages; each extend field carries a per-kind name so that the fully-qualified extension names remain unique within the protowire.schema.v1 package. Numbers 1319 and 1320 are intentionally not used by this allocation because the SBE annotations (sbe.schema_id, sbe.version) already occupy them on FileOptions, and an extension number may be used only once per extended message.

Numbers 1332 through 1346 are reserved for future schema-extension carriers and MUST NOT be allocated by user schemas. Renumbering any of the above allocations is a wire break per the rules defined in STABILITY.md of 's source repository.

section.name: Choosing the Argument Member
section.t: An annotation argument lowers into one member of AnnotationArg's value oneof (string_value, int_value, double_value, bool_value, bytes_value, literal, expression), and a list element into the matching member of LiteralValue. Which member is decided by type, never by the literal's magnitude or content:

list.t: For a parameter with a declared type, the declaration decides. The argument MUST be converted to that type; a literal the type cannot hold is a compile error.

For a parameter declared any, the argument is first typed by its own literal (1e19 is a float because it is spelled as one; "x" is a string) and then converted to the type of the element the annotation is attached to — the field, enum value, or method. For a list, each element is converted to the annotated field's element type. A literal that cannot be converted in kind or in range is a compile error. Where there is no such type (a message-, service-, enum-, or file-level annotation), the literal's own type stands.

A literal no member can represent is a compile error, not a different member. An integer past int_value's 64-bit range MUST NOT be carried as double_value (the member would depend on the magnitude) and MUST NOT be wrapped.
bytes_value carries the literal's own octets verbatim; a consumer MUST NOT decode it again.

section.t: The canonical conformance corpus pins one cell of this rule per field in testdata/schema-extensions/10_literal_args.proto, with the lowered member recorded in 11_literal_carrier_golden.textproto.

section.name: Backward Compatibility with Stock Protocol Buffers Tooling
section.t: The carrier extensions are well-formed Protocol Buffers extensions per . Implementations not importing protowire/proto/schema/v1/descriptor.proto MUST preserve the carrier options as opaque unknown-field bytes across decode/re-encode cycles, in accordance with the standard Protocol Buffers extension semantics.
Implementations that DO import the descriptor file decode the carriers as typed messages.

section.name: Cross-Runtime Considerations
section.t: A schema using function declarations does not, by itself, specify which runtime engine evaluates them. The engine is selected per project at validator-binary build time; this revision specifies that for a given project, at most one engine MAY be active.

Function bodies MUST be registered with the engine at initialization time, keyed by the function's fully-qualified name. An engine encountering a referenced function name with no registered body MUST either:

list.t: refuse to start (strict mode), or
substitute a registered fallback that returns (false, V) with V bearing code "unimplemented" (lenient mode).

section.t: The default mode is implementation-defined; the contract this document specifies is that one of the two behaviors MUST be exhibited.

section.name: Engine Configuration
section.t: Project-level engine selection lives in a text-format Protocol Buffers file named protowire.config.textproto at the project root, carrying exactly one protowire.schema.config.v1.EngineConfig message (schema: protowire/proto/schema/config/v1/config.proto in the protowire source repository). The message lists function-library and catalog-library imports, sets strict_validation (), the default execution mode (), and max_recursion_depth ().

Discovery is nearest-config-wins, walking from the compilation's working directory upward; configurations are never merged. Precedence, highest first: explicit command-line flags; a --config file argument; a config file named by the PROTOWIRE_CONFIG environment variable; the discovered file; built-in defaults (lenient verification, collect-all mode). The engine field is reserved: the expression language is fixed (), so nothing selects an engine; validators MUST ignore the field and tooling SHOULD warn when it is set.

section.name: Multi-Runtime Schemas
section.t: A schema intended to validate identically across multiple consuming runtimes (for example, server-side in a Go validator and client-side in a Java validator) MUST limit its function references to those for which equivalent implementations are registered in every consuming runtime. This is an operational concern; this document does not provide a mechanism for enforcing it at schema declaration time. Implementations MAY provide a portability-check mode that warns or errors on non-portable references.

section.name: Response Envelope
section.t: The Envelope message provides a uniform response carrier across wire formats. Its schema is defined in package envelope.v1:
Semantics:

list.t: status carries an HTTP or gRPC status code.
transport_error is set when no application-layer response was produced (network error, timeout, connection refused). Implementations MUST NOT set transport_error and error simultaneously.

data is the success payload, encoded in whichever wire form the surrounding transport selects (PXF, PB, JSON). Decoders MUST treat data as opaque bytes; it is parsed only after the envelope itself is parsed.

error.code and details[*].code are machine-readable identifiers; clients perform localization by consulting a string table keyed by "error.<code>" and "field.<code>" and substituting args positionally.

section.t: The package path "envelope.v1" is part of the wire contract. Incompatible changes MUST bump the package to "envelope.v2"; "v1" and "v2" MAY coexist indefinitely.

section.name: Decoder Conformance
section.t: This section specifies the requirements that any protowire decoder operating on attacker-controlled bytes MUST satisfy.
The threat model assumes:

list.t: the attacker controls every byte of the input,
the attacker controls the input length, up to a configured maximum,
the attacker MAY submit many inputs concurrently from many sources,
the schema (.proto descriptor, SBE template) and the configured limits are NOT attacker-controlled.

section.t: Under these conditions, a conforming decoder MUST terminate in time and memory bounded by the input length and the configured limits only. It MUST NOT crash, abort, or unwind the host process; it MUST NOT allocate beyond the configured budget; it MUST NOT return string-typed fields whose contents are not valid UTF-8.

section.name: Mandatory Limits
section.t: Conforming decoders MUST enforce the following limits. Defaults are recommended; the values are configurable per call by the calling application except where noted.

texttable.c: PXF block/list nesting; PB submessage / group / map-entry nesting, a big-number message bound to a native number excepted ()
Total input length to a single decode call

Significant digits of any PXF numeric literal's mantissa, its exponent and precision suffix not counted; magnitude of pxf.Decimal.scale on the PB wire; the digit count N a pxf.BigFloat precision suffix implies, and the same N for a pxf.BigFloat's prec on the PB wire
Magnitude of a pxf.BigFloat value's binary exponent, from the PB wire or a PXF literal
Decoded byte length of any PXF b"..." literal
Every PB varint read. NOT configurable.
Element count of any repeated, map, or SBE group field

section.t: A decoder presented with input that requires exceeding any limit MUST return an error before allocating memory proportional to the violating quantity. It MUST NOT abort, panic, raise an uncatchable exception, or unwind into a state from which the caller cannot recover.
Length arithmetic MUST be performed in 64-bit unsigned arithmetic and checked against the buffer length before any narrowing conversion to a native integer width and before any allocation.

Arbitrary-precision magnitudes. MaxNumericLiteralDigits counts the significant digits of a literal's mantissa only: an exponent is bounded by MaxBigFloatExponent and a precision suffix by the N it implies, and a producer writes up to MaxNumericLiteralDigits significant digits plus both (issue #410). It also bounds the magnitude of pxf.Decimal.scale as encoded over PB (): a scale is a digit count, and a decoder that materialises the value computes 10^scale, which costs time and memory proportional to a quantity the input sets directly. A decoder MUST reject a Decimal whose scale magnitude exceeds the limit before materialising anything. MaxBigFloatExponent bounds a pxf.BigFloat (issue #281). The bound is on the value's binary exponent: the wire exponent plus the bit length of the mantissa, so that value = m × 2^e with m in [0.5, 1), and a zero mantissa has none. It is not on the wire field alone, which shifts with the precision a producer chose. Storing a large exponent is cheap, but rendering the value in decimal is not: in the implementations measured, the work grows with the square of the exponent's magnitude, and a five-byte wire exponent or a thirteen-byte literal ("1e646456992") sets it. A decoder MUST reject a BigFloat whose binary exponent exceeds MaxBigFloatExponent in magnitude before materialising it, whether it arrives on the PB wire or as the value of a PXF literal. It MUST likewise reject a BigFloat whose prec implies more digits than MaxNumericLiteralDigits, the bound a precision suffix has (prec above 13603 at the default, ), before allocating anything for it. A producer writes the mantissa widened to prec bits, so without this bound an eleven-byte message stating prec 2^31-1 re-encodes to 256 MiB, past MaxMessageSize. With it, every BigFloat a decoder accepts can also be written as a literal (issue #499), but one: the bound is checked on the mantissa as it arrives, and rounding that mantissa to prec bits can carry the value to the next power of two, one past the bound. Such a value is valid on the wire and MUST be accepted by a PB decoder, as a Decimal with no spelling is. A producer of PXF text that meets it, or a value past either bound, MUST fail with an error. Both bounds, on a Decimal's scale and on a BigFloat's exponent, apply where a value is materialised, not where its fields are read. A decoder that stores a Decimal or BigFloat message's fields without computing its value, such as a PXF decoder reading the block form ("f { mantissa = ... exponent = ... }"), or a protobuf decoder reading the message as plain fields, is not subject to them, because storing the fields costs only what the input's length already bounds. A decoder that does compute the value, in whatever form it arrived, MUST apply the bound first. A value past a bound can therefore be decoded field by field, but a producer of PXF text still fails on it, so it is never written back out as a literal (issue #281; protowire-go#188). The default, 16384, is the exponent range of IEEE 754 binary128, and admits every literal up to about 1e±4932. Rendering a BigFloat inside the bound is the consumer's operation, and where the result is a PXF literal it is bounded by MaxNumericLiteralDigits like any other literal. The bound applies to a literal's value after rounding to the precision it is read at, not to its exact decimal value: a finite decimal literal cannot hold a power of two exactly, so the literal of a value at 2^±MaxBigFloatExponent may lie just past the bound, and rounding brings it back (issue #410). A numeric literal, or a big-number message, whose value the decoder's arbitrary-precision type cannot represent MUST be rejected with an error; a decoder MUST NOT substitute an infinity or a truncated value.

The two bounds MaxNumericLiteralDigits states are independent: the scale bound limits the work a PB decoder performs, the digit bound limits the length of a text literal, and neither implies the other. A big number MAY therefore be representable on the wire and have no PXF spelling: BigInt.abs and Decimal.unscaled are bounded on the wire only by MaxMessageSize, and a Decimal at a scale of -MaxNumericLiteralDigits renders its unscaled digits followed by that many zeros, one digit more than the digit bound. A Decimal at a positive scale has a spelling at the bound ("0.000...1"): leading zeros are not significant, so the digit bound does not count them (issue #410, reversing in part the reading of issue #310). A producer of PXF text (a marshaller, or a binder rendering a (pxf.default) carrier) that meets such a value MUST fail with an error rather than truncate, round or change notation; the wire value itself remains valid and MUST be accepted by a PB decoder.

section.name: Recursion
section.t: PXF parsers descend recursively into "{...}" blocks and "[...]" lists; PB parsers descend into submessages, groups, and map entries. Conforming decoders MUST:

list.t: maintain a depth counter incremented at every recursive descent;
reject input that would cause the counter to exceed MaxNestingDepth;

thread the depth counter through inner decoder instances constructed mid-stream. In particular, when a nested submessage is decoded by handing its bytes to a freshly constructed input-stream object, the depth counter MUST be passed in rather than reset to zero.

section.t: A pxf.BigInt, pxf.Decimal or pxf.BigFloat message that a decoder binds to a native arbitrary-precision number is a value, not a recursive descent, as its PXF literal is: the decoder reads it as one field and descends into nothing. A struct at depth MaxNestingDepth may therefore hold one. Read as a message of plain fields, as a generic protobuf decoder or the PXF block form reads it, it is a submessage and counts as one (protowire-cpp#148).

A producer of PXF text or of PB MUST fail with an error on a message nested more deeply than MaxNestingDepth, counted as a decoder reading its output would count it, rather than write a document that a decoder at the same limit rejects (issue #502). The limit is configurable per call, as a decoder's is. Such a message can only come from somewhere other than a conforming decoder at that limit, such as a language value built in memory or a protobuf runtime with a higher limit, and a producer that follows a reference cycle meets the limit instead of exhausting its stack.

section.name: UTF-8 Enforcement
section.t: Proto3 string fields are sequences of valid UTF-8 . Conforming decoders:

list.t: MUST validate UTF-8 strictly when populating any string-typed field, regardless of the source encoding (PB length-delimited bytes, SBE char-array fields, SBE varData, PXF simple-string or triple-string).
MUST NOT use UTF-8 decoders that substitute U+FFFD for invalid sequences when populating string-typed fields.

MUST reject PXF \xHH and \NNN (octal) escapes that produce invalid UTF-8 when the surrounding literal is bound to a string-typed field. The same byte sequences are permitted inside b"..." (bytes literal) and inside string literals bound to bytes-typed fields.
MUST reject PXF \uHHHH and \UHHHHHHHH escapes that encode a surrogate code point or a code point above U+10FFFF.

section.name: SBE Bounds Checking
section.t: The bounds-checking obligations in are conformance requirements, restated here for emphasis. Specifically:

list.t: Wire block length less than template block length MUST be rejected ().
Group count multiplied by group block length MUST be 64-bit checked against the buffer length before iteration ().
A group with count > 0 and wire_block_length == 0 MUST be rejected before any per-element allocation ().

section.name: Map Keys
section.t: In implementation languages where dynamic property assignment walks a prototype chain (notably JavaScript / TypeScript), a conforming decoder MUST NOT use a plain object literal as the container for attacker-keyed maps. Such decoders MUST use a prototype-free object (Object.create(null)) or a Map, or MUST explicitly reject the keys "__proto__", "constructor", and "prototype". The same obligation applies in any other implementation language that exhibits prototype-mutation semantics for reserved string keys.

section.name: Validation Engine Conformance
section.t: A protowire implementation that ships a validation engine for the schema language extensions MUST:

list.t: implement the presence semantics specified in ;
emit Violations whose shape conforms to the structure defined in ;
enrich emitted Violations with at minimum the fields listed in ;
operate in collect-all mode by default;
accept registration of function bodies by fully-qualified name;
either refuse to start or substitute a documented fallback when a referenced function has no registered body.

section.t: An implementation MAY ship without a validation engine; in that case the implementation processes the schema's declarations for purposes unrelated to validation (e.g., code generation) and MUST NOT silently fail validation rules.

The dispatch draft registers both. Neither carries protowire's additional decoder-conformance and annotation-extension constraints. section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: The protowire family is designed to be parsed safely on attacker-controlled bytes. specifies the conformance requirements that follow from this objective. This section addresses the considerations that do not reduce to a single conformance requirement.

Resource exhaustion. Without the limits in , every protowire encoding admits trivial denial-of-service inputs: deeply nested PXF blocks blow native call stacks; large PB length prefixes drive allocator pressure; SBE group counts multiplied by element sizes overflow length arithmetic; long PXF numeric literals drive quadratic big-number parsers. Implementers MUST apply .

Length-arithmetic overflow. All offset, length, and count arithmetic on attacker-supplied quantities MUST use 64-bit unsigned operations and MUST be checked against the input length before any narrowing. Implementations in languages whose default integer width on the host platform is 32 bits MUST be particularly careful to use explicit 64-bit types.

Trapping conversions. Several implementation languages provide integer conversions that abort the process on out-of-range input (Swift Int(:), Rust "as" without checked*, Java Math.toIntExact, C++ static_cast with subsequent UB). When converting attacker-supplied lengths or counts to native integer widths, implementations MUST use fallible conversion forms.

UTF-8 substitution. Many platform string APIs silently substitute U+FFFD for invalid UTF-8. When such substitution is applied to a string-typed field, the resulting message violates the proto3 invariant that string fields contain valid UTF-8 and may differ from the producer's intent. Implementations MUST use strict, error-returning UTF-8 decoders on string fields ().

Schema input. An implementation that accepts a FileDescriptorSet or SBE schema XML at runtime, where the descriptor or XML is, or may be, attacker-controlled, MUST apply the limits of to the schema parser as well. XML schema parsers MUST disable DTDs and external entities to mitigate XXE attacks (e.g. defusedxml in Python; XmlReaderSettings.DtdProcessing = Prohibit in .NET; the feature flags "disallow-doctype-decl", "external-general-entities", and "external-parameter-entities" in Java).

Prototype pollution. Decoders implemented in JavaScript, TypeScript, or any language with prototype-mutation semantics for reserved string keys MUST avoid plain object literals as the storage for attacker-keyed maps; see .

Cryptographic transport. This document specifies an encoding family. It does not provide confidentiality, integrity, or origin authentication; transports carrying protowire payloads SHOULD use TLS or an equivalent.

Application-level error metadata. AppError.metadata () is a free-form string-to-string map. Servers SHOULD NOT place sensitive information (credentials, raw user input) in metadata. Clients SHOULD treat metadata values as untrusted and apply context-appropriate sanitization before display or logging.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps

abstract.t: This document defines a date and time format for use in Internet protocols that is a profile of the ISO 8601 standard for representation of dates and times using the Gregorian calendar.

front.title: UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646

abstract.t: ISO/IEC 10646-1 defines a large character set called the Universal Character Set (UCS) which encompasses most of the world's writing systems. The originally proposed encodings of the UCS, however, were not compatible with many current applications and protocols, and this has led to the development of UTF-8, the object of this memo. UTF-8 has the characteristic of preserving the full US-ASCII range, providing compatibility with file systems, parsers and other software that rely on US-ASCII values but are transparent to other values. This memo obsoletes and replaces RFC 2279.

front.title: The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings

abstract.t: This document describes the commonly used base 64, base 32, and base 16 encoding schemes. It also discusses the use of line-feeds in encoded data, use of padding in encoded data, use of non-alphabet characters in encoded data, use of different encoding alphabets, and canonical encodings. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF

abstract.t: Internet technical specifications often need to define a formal syntax. Over the years, a modified version of Backus-Naur Form (BNF), called Augmented BNF (ABNF), has been popular among many Internet specifications. The current specification documents ABNF. It balances compactness and simplicity with reasonable representational power. The differences between standard BNF and ABNF involve naming rules, repetition, alternatives, order-independence, and value ranges. This specification also supplies additional rule definitions and encoding for a core lexical analyzer of the type common to several Internet specifications. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Media Type Specifications and Registration Procedures

abstract.t: This document defines procedures for the specification and registration of media types for use in HTTP, MIME, and other Internet protocols. This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice.

front.title: Case-Sensitive String Support in ABNF

abstract.t: This document extends the base definition of ABNF (Augmented Backus-Naur Form) to include a way to specify US-ASCII string literals that are matched in a case-sensitive manner.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

front.title: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format

abstract.t: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a lightweight, text-based, language-independent data interchange format. It was derived from the ECMAScript Programming Language Standard. JSON defines a small set of formatting rules for the portable representation of structured data.
This document removes inconsistencies with other specifications of JSON, repairs specification errors, and offers experience-based interoperability guidance.

front.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

abstract.t: This document specifies version 1.3 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol. TLS allows client/server applications to communicate over the Internet in a way that is designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery.
This document updates RFCs 5705 and 6066, and obsoletes RFCs 5077, 5246, and 6961. This document also specifies new requirements for TLS 1.2 implementations.

front.title: HTTP Semantics

abstract.t: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems. This document describes the overall architecture of HTTP, establishes common terminology, and defines aspects of the protocol that are shared by all versions. In this definition are core protocol elements, extensibility mechanisms, and the "http" and "https" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.
